The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

A Fort Pierce man is facing an aggravated assault charge after two tow trucks were hit with a U-Haul truck. On Thursday, Fort Pierce Police officers responded to the 5400 block of Jamboree Drive, east of Interstate 95, regarding a report of a U-Haul box truck crashing into two vehicles. Officers learned that the U-Haul had been parked in violation of homeowner association restrictions, and the contracted tow company was attempting to remove it. During the tow attempt, the person intervened, police said. A second tow truck was positioned behind the U-Haul to prevent it from leaving. After the person refused to pay a drop fee, he entered the U-Haul, backed off the tow truck and struck the tow truck parked behind him, police said. He then continued to drive forward and reverse repeatedly until he freed the U-Haul from between the two vehicles, police said. The person drove down the street, where responding officers located him shortly afterward. No injuries were reported. The U-Haul was towed and the man was taken to the St. Police didn't identify him. Lucie County voters assigned to Precincts 39 and 52 will cast their ballots at a temporary polling place for the Nov. 3 general election because of renovations at their usual location. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced on Tuesday that voters in the two precincts will move from the Spanish Lakes Country Club clubhouse to Lakewood Park Church, 5405 Turnpike Feeder Road in Fort Pierce. See also: Suspected smuggling case leads to arrests as boat is removed and migrants face processing Walker encouraged voters to take advantage of early voting, including at the county’s newest early voting site, Lakewood Park Branch Library, to avoid Election Day lines. Early voting runs from Oct. to 6 p.m., at these locations: Lakewood Park Branch Library, 7605 Santa Barbara Drive, Fort Pierce Renaissance Business Park, 4132 Okeechobee Road, Fort Pierce Zora Neale Hurston Library, 3008 Avenue D, Fort Pierce MIDFlorida Credit Union Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, Port St. Lucie Community Center, 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lewis Library, 2950 Rosser Blvd., Port St. Lucie Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence, 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Minsky Gym, 750 SW Darwin Blvd., Port St. Lucie The deadline to request a vote-by-mail ballot is Oct. Voters returning ballots by mail are encouraged to do so at least seven days before Election Day. Vote-by-mail ballots can also be dropped off at any early voting site or at these Supervisor of Elections locations: Renaissance Business Park, 4132 Okeechobee Road, Fort Pierce St. Lucie West South County Annex, 250 NW Country Club Drive, Port St. Conrad Administration Annex, 1664 SE Walton Road, Port St. Lucie Tradition Tax Collector, 10264 SW Village Parkway, Port St.

Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

While many people are just beginning to think about the holidays, volunteers with Back to Basics are already hard at work making sure thousands of Palm Beach County children have gifts to open this Christmas.The nonprofit's annual Angel Program provides new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy to children in need throughout the county. "We provide new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy for all of them."Because of the large number of children served, preparations begin months before the holiday season arrives. Some gifts are already being sorted and wrapped as volunteers work to get ahead of the demand."The biggest part of our program is we can depend on the community to adopt these children," Kelly said. "About 7,000 will go out to the community each year and the rest of them we do in-house."The organization is encouraging local residents, businesses and civic groups to participate by adopting children, donating gifts or volunteering their time.Back to Basics is also celebrating another successful community initiative. The nonprofit recently completed its annual school uniform drive, which provided approximately 20,000 uniforms to students at more than 60 elementary and middle schools throughout Palm Beach County."We serve over 60 schools here in Palm Beach County," said board member Mike O'Dell. "Many of the children who go to school are required to have uniforms, and they just don't have the financial wherewithal to do that."Volunteers say community support is essential to the success of both programs and helps ensure local children have the resources they need to thrive both in school and during the holiday season."You're helping those in need, and this is a great way to have your children learn the generosity and the joy of giving," Santa Claus joked during WPTV's Shining A Light visit.As the holiday season approaches, Back to Basics hopes more people will step forward to help make Christmas brighter for thousands of Palm Beach County children.

Kyler Murray and the Minnesota Vikings' offense would've appreciated a touchdown for their progress down the stretch, but there was only one way to truly secure this victory.T.J. Hockenson fittingly took the winning slide.The Vikings stayed undefeated with more dominance by their defense and five field goals from Will Reichard, sidestepping their early passing game problems to beat the winless Miami Dolphins 15-10 on Sunday.Hockenson tied a career high with 13 receptions for 119 yards on 13 targets from Murray, including the game-sealing 8-yard catch on third-and-5 from the 10. The eighth-year tight end was wide open and could've coasted into the end zone, but he wisely slid in front of the goal line to drain the clock to the two-minute warning."Once you get the first down, you've got to get down," said Hockenson, who had his highest yardage total since Week 10 of the 2023 season. I saw that goal line and I wanted it, but it's for the betterment of the team that we ended on offense."With the Dolphins out of timeouts, the Vikings had Murray take three straight kneel-downs to move to 4-0 for the second time in three years — despite going without a touchdown in two games."If we want to score, we should do it earlier," Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell said.Murray finished 27 for 37 for 247 yards without a turnover, but he took four sacks for 34 yards against a Dolphins defense that had none in the first three games and was often tentative and unsteady in the pocket until Hockenson helped him open up the field with a handful of clutch and difficult catches.The Dolphins, who are 0-4 for the first time since starting 0-7 in 2019 in their first season under then-coach Brian Flores, were crushed by a combination of unforced mistakes — including nine penalties for 55 yards.New Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis went just 9 for 17 for 85 yards, losing a fumble during one of the two sacks by Dallas Turner. The four teams the Dolphins have faced in coach Jeff Hafley's first year are 15-1."You hate the feeling of continuing to get better without actually gaining wins on the win column, but as we see, we're going out there and competing," Willis said.Willis thought he had escaped the relentless Vikings pass rush to float a 68-yard touchdown pass to Chris Bell early in the second quarter, but Bell was flagged for illegal touching after stepping out of bounds as he moved to get open.The Vikings had 11 penalties for 85 yards, but they dodged one when Ivan Pace Jr. had a call for roughing the kicker waved off by the video replay assist system's determination that he tipped Bradley Pinion's punt and therefore didn't commit a penalty.After netting just 76 yards on 21 plays in the first half and failing to finish any possession across midfield, the Dolphins finally found a couple of creases in Minnesota's suffocating defense directed by Flores.Ollie Gordon, in an elevated role following the season-ending knee injury to star running back De'Vone Achane, ripped off a career-best 53-yard run on third-and-5 to set up Riley Patterson's 27-yard field goal. Gordon, who ended the game with 100 yards rushing, had a 12-yard touchdown run on the next drive to pull the Dolphins within 12-10.Reichard, who stretched the NFL's longest active streak to 31 consecutive made field goals, drew a loud roar when he was shown on the videoboard during the two-minute warning. Murray, on the other hand, heard some mild rounds of boos as the unproductive possessions began to pile up.But the Vikings had the ball for 14 of 15 minutes in the fourth quarter, accumulating eight first downs.Aaron Jones also carried another heavy load with 20 carries for 94 yards and four receptions for 34 yards, with the Vikings missing star wide receiver Justin Jefferson (ankle) for the first time since Week 12 of the 2023 season and running back Jordan Mason (thumb) for the third game in a row."That door will get kicked down soon," Murray said.The Vikings played most of the second half without two of their best blockers. Left guard Donovan Jackson (knee) was sidelined in the first quarter and left tackle Christian Darrisaw (neck) was hurt in the second after going head-first into the pile at the end of a run. Darrisaw returned after halftime, only to be pulled again as a precaution for a concussion evaluation following a second hit.Dolphins: Host Cincinnati next Sunday.Vikings: Play at New Orleans next Sunday.

It takes an army of 38 staff members to create all the video, replays, and entertainment fans enjoy at Florida Panthers games at Amerant Bank Arena.WPTV Florida Panthers Anchor and Panthers 360 Mike Trim went one-on-one with Mike Masino, vice president of entertainment and operations, who gave Trim a tour of the newly renovated control room and front-of-house operations.WATCH: Newly renovated control room at Amerant Bank Arena brings Panthers games to lifeThe front-of-house operations area serves as the hub of game-day activity. It houses the public address announcer, primary producer, music operations, a spotter, and a gold horn operator. Lighting operations and building lights are also managed from the same space, along with social media stations used for interactive fan games."Yeah, so this is our front-of-house operations area. This is where we have our public address announcer. We have our primary producer, music operations, our spotter, and our gold horn operator. We've got our lighting operations team as well as building lights. And then up here we have some of our fun stuff. We've got social media stations for some of our interactive games," Mike Masino said.What is now one open workspace was once 3 separate rooms."This was actually 3 rooms," Masino said."Flow communication becomes a lot easier. Direct line of sight is also helpful, and it actually created some more space for the operators," Masino said.The tour also included the broadcast control room — the engine room of the entire production."Now we've got the actual broadcast control room; this is where the real magic happens," Masino said.Inside, Mark serves as the technical director, and Scott is the director. Masino compared the director's role to one familiar to those in television news."Mark who's TDing, and you've got Scott who is our director. Our director, just like in news, they're actually calling the cameras, calling the angles. Queuing videos," Masino said.When Trim asked how the team handles milestone moments — whether anticipated or unexpected — Masino said the control room is always plugged in and prepared."We're directly plugged in with our public relations team and our communications team who communicates that milestone to us. We're prepared ahead of time," Masino said.Masino noted that the 38-person team is a critical part of the operation, pointing to significant growth in both staff size and talent."We've doubled the staff. Talent level is continuing to increase every year, and it's really become a wonderful, wonderful team," Masino said."They're on it. They're locked in all game, but it's what they do, and it's what they love to do," Masino said.The first pre-season game for the Panthers also marked a significant technology upgrade for the arena."So tonight's actually a milestone for us, moving from a baseband video infrastructure where you're hard patching cables to a networked routable video infrastructure," Masino said."All of our cabling throughout the building was replaced to bring us to the highest quality broadcast infrastructure that sports are doing these days," Masino said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Florida center Aleksander Barkov has been placed on long-term injured reserve by the Panthers, meaning the injury to his left leg will keep him sidelined for at least the next 10 games and quite possibly beyond.The Panthers are still unclear on the extent of Barkov's injury, coach Paul Maurice said, adding that Barkov will see Florida team physicians on Monday.>> RELATED: More Panthers news"We know it’s going to be 10 (games) anyway," Maurice said after the Panthers practiced in Irvine, California. "We’ll see what they say Monday. Whatever they say."Florida made a pair of roster additions after placing Barkov on the injured list Saturday, bringing up center Sam Lafferty and defenseman Alexander Petrovic.Barkov was hurt midway through the second period of Florida's 4-3 overtime loss to the San Jose Sharks on Thursday night. He was jostling for the puck along the boards, got pushed by the Sharks' Darnell Nurse and awkwardly fell to the ice with his left leg at an unnatural angle. It appeared his knee buckled on the play.Barkov remained down for a few moments, then got up and headed toward the tunnel leading to the Florida dressing room. He walked with a bit of a limp and appeared to angrily try to throw off his gloves as he moved toward the room.Barkov — Florida's captain and a huge part of the Panthers' runs to Stanley Cup championships in 2024 and 2025 — missed the entire 2025-26 season with torn ligaments in his right knee. He went scoreless in his first two appearance of this season for Florida, which plays Sunday at Anaheim.There was some good injury news Saturday, with Maurice saying that forward Brad Marchand is getting closer to making his season debut — "real close," Maurice said — and that defenseman Gustav Forsling, who had the overtime goal in the opener at Carolina but was a last-minute scratch at San Jose with an upper body issue, is a game-time decision for Sunday.

A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community.The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million.The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. “That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women,” said Pietrewicz.After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on.“We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately,” she said.WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it.The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors.“You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals,” said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging.Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location.But some seniors say the location itself is important.“That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community,” Pietrewicz said.Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live.“We live here, we want rights to do thing, besides trouble,” Lovett said.The Council on Aging said it understands those concerns, but says change is necessary.For now, the Council on Aging says services at the Orange Avenue center are continuing. There is no finalized timeline for the closure because the transition is tied to the sale of the property.“We understand the concerns, it's a change for us too. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change,” Smith said.The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St.

President Trump announced that more than 20 million seniors on Medicare will soon receive a direct deposit of nearly $100, drawing Democratic criticism and questions about whether the payments — made without congressional approval — are legal."I am pleased to announce over 20 million seniors on Medicare will still be receiving a deposit of nearly $100 directly into their bank accounts," Trump said.RELATED STORY | Trump announces $500 refunds for nearly 1 million 'Obamacare' enrolleesTrump said the money will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. A White House fact sheet says most eligible seniors will receive $90 via direct deposit in early October. Those without direct deposit will receive a check.The Medicare payment is not the only check the administration is cutting. Last month, Trump announced refunds to some people enrolled in Affordable Care Act health plans, saying they had been previously overcharged."Nearly 1 million hardworking Americans in 30 states will soon be getting refunds of $500 each," Trump said.On the campaign trail, Trump has also promised more money if Republicans win in the November midterm elections.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | $5K reality check: Experts say Trump's promise of midterm checks would strain the economySo far, no legal challenge has resulted in a court blocking either the $500 ACA refunds or the $90 Medicare payments, though Democrats have been sharply critical of both."If you want to BUY midterm votes, maybe start by not gutting everyone's health care in the first place," Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden said, referring to the $500 ACA checks.Also drawing scrutiny on Capitol Hill is Trump's use of taxpayer dollars to pay for commercials this campaign season. The White House says the spending is legal, but others disagree. Complaints have been filed with the FCC and broadcasters, though no judge has yet blocked the commercials from airing.

The Florida Highway Patrol is at the scene of a deadly incident. According to FHP, the crash was reported on Monday, Oct. near the intersection of State Road A1A and Regatta Drive in Vero Beach. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 A Florida Highway Patrol spokesperson provided additional details on the crash on Monday night. A Freightliner roll-off truck that was operated by a 25-year-old man from Fort Pierce was traveling south on A1A, approaching Regatta Drive and slowing for traffic ahead. An Isuzu box truck driven by a 53-year-old man from Fort Pierce, was traveling south on A1A behind the roll-off truck. According to FHP, the driver of the Isuzu box truck failed to slow in time. As a result, the front of the box truck collided with the rear of the roll-off truck. The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations.One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it.Watch report from Katie Lagrone"We have one fatality of a beautiful high school girl. It's just heartbreaking," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing.Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash.Florida law requires school buses built since 2001 to be equipped with seat belts. However, students are not required to wear them, and state law does not require the more protective lap-and-shoulder belts recommended by federal safety investigators. Instead, many Florida school buses continue to use standard lap belts.The federal recommendation followed an investigation by investigative reporter Katie LaGrone more than a decade ago.In 2012, a St. Lucie County school bus collided with a semi-truck, killing 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash.Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety.The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. Simulations demonstrated that lap-and-shoulder belts provide greater protection by better controlling a passenger's movement during a crash.As a result, the NTSB recommended that all school buses nationwide be equipped with lap-and-shoulder belts.The NTSB specifically urged Florida to change state law to require lap-and-shoulder belts on new large school buses.That recommendation was never adopted.Today, it remains unclear how many Florida school districts have voluntarily upgraded their fleets to meet the federal recommendation.In St. Lucie County, nearly 15 years after Aaron's death, about 20% of district school buses still use only standard lap belts.In Polk County, a district spokesperson confirmed on Monday that all the district’s school buses are equipped with just lap belts.The latest crash has renewed questions about whether stronger seat belt requirements could better protect students who are traveling to and from school on a school bus.Despite the concerns raised by this tragedy, transportation safety experts continue to emphasize that deadly school bus crashes are extremely rare, and that school buses remain the safest form of transportation for students traveling to and from school.For families in Polk County and across Florida, the crash could prompt renewed scrutiny of whether the state's school bus safety standards should be updated to reflect federal recommendations."No one will ever understand how heavy this weighs on our hearts," Polk County Schools Superintendent Fred Heid said following the crash.

Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point.Signs lined the street as protesters chanted "no more bullying" and "hold bullies accountable," rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy.WATCH BELOW: Parents demand action after girl jumps from school busLast week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video.Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life."I thank God he gave me another chance to live," Estrella said, holding back tears.Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired."What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?" Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change."I just hope there's justice and the students responsible," said Estela Meras. "Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

The political committee supporting Amendment 3 — which would raise Florida's homestead tax exemption — received an $18 million cash infusion in September, campaign finance records show. The two committees opposing the amendment raised a combined $680,000, a margin of more than 26 to 1.In the coming days and weeks, voters can expect to see significant messaging urging a "yes" vote on the amendment.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 backers outraise opponents 26-to-1Digging deeper into those campaign finance records, I found the "No" committees received donations from numerous corporate, individual and nonprofit contributors. Yes on 3's $18 million came from a single source: Florida Realtors.Margy Grant is the chief executive of Florida Realtors and the sole contributor to "Yes on 3.""As the voice of real estate, Florida Realtors is a longtime advocate for homeowners," Grant said. "Families are struggling with the affordability of so many things. When you go to the grocery store, when you go to the gas station, prices just continue to climb. The one thing we can possibly control is property taxes." Jackson Peel, spokesman for "Floridians for Shared Prosperity" — one of the two "No" groups — said his side has an advantage despite the funding gap."Well, we have the advantage of the facts on our side," Peel said. "This is not the savings that is promised on the mailers in your mailbox from the realtors— that this is a scam and a tax shift. You're gonna end up paying more in other ways."While the political committees against Amendment 3 have a much smaller war chest, Peel said Florida voters are still hearing their warnings through opposition from groups like the Florida Sheriff's Association and the Florida Association of Firefighters."I'm on the side of the sheriffs, the police, and the firefighters who say that this is bad for our community's public safety. I'm on the side of the teachers who say, yeah, this is gonna cut after-school programs that help our kids." Peel said.On the question of funding for public services, Grant said she has full confidence in elected officials."If you look at the increase in revenue over the past 10 years, it has doubled. Services have not doubled," Grant said. "I have full faith and confidence in our elected officials that they will be able to implement Amendment 3 successfully and effectively." A constitutional amendment requires approval by 60 percent of voters to pass. Pete Polls found 45 percent of likely voters support Amendment 3, 30 percent oppose it, and 25 percent say they are undecided.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

A 17-year-old was killed in a Fellsmere shooting Friday night after a meetup of more than 100 teens turned violent, according to the sheriff. The shooting happened at around 11:24 p.m. at Garcia’s Boat Ramp , where about 100 teens had gathered. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the group included teens ages 14 to 19, with drinking and fighting reported. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. But now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix. CBS12 confirmed with the family that the slain 17-year-old was Sulliman Bah, a senior at Sebastian River High School. He and a group of friends approached a pickup truck with two 18-year-olds inside. The Bah opened the door and attempted to punch someone inside when a shot was fired. See also: What Florida voters need to know about the 3 constitutional amendments on the Nov. ballot Bah, who was shot, was taken by friends toward Fellsmere. Deputies and EMS met them at Fellsmere City Hall and performed CPR before he was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later transported to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he succumbed to his injuries. No arrests have been made. Flowers said the driver and passenger inside the truck have cooperated with investigators and turned over the truck and firearm. The sheriff said the preliminary investigation indicates a self-defense claim may apply. We will be submitting a warrant in the case, but at this time it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim as a result, Flowers said. The sheriff said the state will ultimately decide whether charges are filed. Investigators used Flock technology to identify people connected to the truck and shooting. Deputies also recovered additional guns and multiple shell casings. Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators.

I visited Love, Hope & Healing Inc. to learn more about IGNITE: The Father & Son Grill Challenge, an event built around mentoring, communication and creating stronger relationships between young men and the adults who support them.While the event includes grilling and friendly competition, organizers say the larger goal is helping fathers, sons, mentors and mentees spend meaningful time together."We will have what we call the Fire Circle, where we will have a therapist-led session, and we're talking about some of these conversations that fathers and sons need to have, but rarely have and don't know how to have," said Donte Bates, co-founder and executive director of Love, Hope & Healing Inc. "So we're creating that space for them to actually talk about it."Yolanda Bates, CEO of Love, Hope & Healing Inc., said events like IGNITE help strengthen relationships that can have a lasting impact on young people."Fathers and sons, they need to create these bonds where these young men can have these experiences and the leadership and mentorship as they grow," she said.One of the organizations supporting the effort is United Way of Palm Beach County. Gwynette Williams, vice president of mentoring, said relationship-building is at the heart of the organization's mission."It's important to make sure that we are building relationships between adults and young people all over Palm Beach County," Williams said. "That's really what we do all day long."Williams also summed up one of the event's unique attractions with a smile."You can't go wrong with men and meat," she said.Mentor Bruce Lewis said his involvement is rooted in helping young men see a positive path forward."It's serving as a positive role model for the young African American males who really need that, giving them a good pathway to success," Lewis said. "I look forward to helping them build their futures."His mentee, Nate, said he's excited about both the experience and the opportunity to grow."I'm looking forward to making friends and having a better bond," he said.The event's presenting partner, Lowe's Home Improvement, is providing a grill and supplies for participating teams."We're in the community, and we're for the community," said David Territo, a Lowe's store manager.ABOUT IGNITE: THE FATHER & SON GRILL CHALLENGEOn Oct. 17, dozens of fathers, father figures, mentors, sons and mentees will gather at Gaines Park Recreation Center in West Palm Beach for IGNITE: The Father & Son Grill Challenge. Organized by Love, Hope & Healing Inc. and supported by Lowe's Home Improvement, the event uses grilling as a way to bring people together, creating opportunities for mentorship, teamwork and meaningful conversations. Along with a hands-on grill challenge, participants will take part in "The Fire Circle," a therapist-led discussion designed to help fathers and sons talk about topics that often go unspoken, from communication and accountability to emotional wellness and support systems. No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. "The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case." The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. "There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. "When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there." Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. "Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." Region Indian River County The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. "The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office. "Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. "I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. The political committee supporting Amendment 3 — which would raise Florida's homestead tax exemption — received an $18 million cash infusion in September, campaign finance records show. The two committees opposing the amendment raised a combined $680,000, a margin of more than 26 to 1.In the coming days and weeks, voters can expect to see significant messaging urging a "yes" vote on the amendment.Digging deeper into those campaign finance records, I found the "No" committees received donations from numerous corporate, individual and nonprofit contributors. Yes on 3's $18 million came from a single source: Florida Realtors.Margy Grant is the chief executive of Florida Realtors and the sole contributor to "Yes on 3.""As the voice of real estate, Florida Realtors is a longtime advocate for homeowners," Grant said. "Families are struggling with the affordability of so many things. When you go to the grocery store, when you go to the gas station, prices just continue to climb. The one thing we can possibly control is property taxes." Jackson Peel, spokesman for "Floridians for Shared Prosperity" — one of the two "No" groups — said his side has an advantage despite the funding gap."Well, we have the advantage of the facts on our side," Peel said. "This is not the savings that is promised on the mailers in your mailbox from the realtors— that this is a scam and a tax shift. You're gonna end up paying more in other ways."While the political committees against Amendment 3 have a much smaller war chest, Peel said Florida voters are still hearing their warnings through opposition from groups like the Florida Sheriff's Association and the Florida Association of Firefighters."I'm on the side of the sheriffs, the police, and the firefighters who say that this is bad for our community's public safety. I'm on the side of the teachers who say, yeah, this is gonna cut after-school programs that help our kids." Services have not doubled," Grant said. "I have full faith and confidence in our elected officials that they will be able to implement Amendment 3 successfully and effectively." A constitutional amendment requires approval by 60 percent of voters to pass.
