No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point.Signs lined the street as protesters chanted "no more bullying" and "hold bullies accountable," rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy.Last week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video.Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life."I thank God he gave me another chance to live," Estrella said, holding back tears.Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired."What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?" Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change."I just hope there's justice and the students responsible," said Estela Meras. "Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

The new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road is now open for drivers in Indian River County, a year ahead of schedule. Ron DeSantis, joined by Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue, held a press conference at 11 a.m. in Vero Beach on Monday announcing the completion of the nearly $100 million project. "This is the first new interchange built in this area, in almost 50 years, so this is going to bring new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit," DeSantis said. DeSantis said the new interchange is expected to reduce congestion on nearby interchanges like Indrio Road and State Road 60, cutting drive times in half. It also aims to improve emergency response efforts and movement along Florida's supply chain. "With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future," DeSantis said. According to FDOT, work began back in August 2023 and was projected to be completed by spring 2027. "We actually implemented voluntary acceleration on this project," Perdue said. "Thank you to Halley Engineering Contractors and team for bringing an idea forward that actually enabled us to finish this project an entire year — to be exact, 400 days — ahead of schedule." While this new interchange is now complete, Perdue said work isn't done just yet on the Treasure Coast, as there are nearly a billion dollars of transportation investment planned for the area that FDOT will continue to work on and finish as quickly as possible. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community.The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million.The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. “That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women,” said Pietrewicz.After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on.“We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately,” she said.WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it.The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors.“You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals,” said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging.Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location.But some seniors say the location itself is important.“That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community,” Pietrewicz said.Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live.“We live here, we want rights to do thing, besides trouble,” Lovett said.The Council on Aging said it understands those concerns, but says change is necessary.For now, the Council on Aging says services at the Orange Avenue center are continuing. There is no finalized timeline for the closure because the transition is tied to the sale of the property.“We understand the concerns, it's a change for us too. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change,” Smith said.The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St.

Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region.

The man accused of crossing state lines and traveling to Indian River County to kill his ex-girlfriend was booked into the Indian River County Jail on Monday. According to Indian River County Jail records, Matthew Waggle, 33, was booked into the Indian River County Jail at around 5:20 a.m. He faces a charge of first-degree murder. CBS12 reported on the August shooting after authorities found the victim's body, identified as Dawn Kriskewic , in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Investigators say Waggle traveled to Vero Beach by bus and Uber before allegedly killing Kriskewic outside her home Sunday morning. See also: FHP: Wrong-way driver caused deadly I-95 crash Sunday near PB Lakes Boulevard Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said surveillance video captured Waggle walking through Kriskewic's neighborhood shortly after an Uber dropped him off. Investigators say Waggle then left the area, taking an Uber back to Orlando before boarding another Greyhound bus. He eventually made his way to West Virginia, where investigators say he hid at a motel. Flowers said at the time that Flock Safety cameras were instrumental in tracking down Waggle. Authorities had later tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him.

Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

Lucie County mosquito control are working to stop mosquitoes from breeding after recent rain created standing water. In a residential neighborhood near U.S. 1 and Fort Pierce, mosquito control teams treated swales and used a backpack blower to distribute larvicide. Officials said the rain has increased standing water, which allows mosquito eggs to hatch. "So relative to last year, mosquito calls have been pretty reduced, but at any moment’s notice following a lot of rain, we can have a huge strike in population, so it's important to be on top of our game," said Daniel Tuzzolino, senior entomologist at St. Lucie County Mosquito Control. DENGUE FEVER: Dengue fever case in Palm Beach County prompts mosquito control action Kenneth Fusco, a nearby resident, shared his experience with the mosquito problem. "If I go out in my front yard and start to do anything, you get bit. I have an island behind me with some cats. If I go over there, I have to wear long pants because I get chewed to death," Fusco said. He added, "Park the truck and leave it for 20 minutes and leave it in front of my house, please!" Crews are also monitoring reports of dengue fever and West Nile virus in surrounding counties. They are asking residents to empty or remove containers holding water to prevent mosquito breeding. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "We are really doubling down and making sure that the people of St. Lucie County know the importance of tipping and tossing because anything that you do to remove potential environment for those dangerous mosquitoes really helps reduce the likelihood that we have transmission in this county," Tuzzolino said. Thursday's heavy rain also caused erosion and a washout along Indian River Drive, where crews were completing a shoulder repair project designed to protect the roadway during heavy rain events. More rain is expected, which could lead to additional standing water and, Tuzzolino said, "A lot more mosquitoes! A lot more mosquitoes!" If you are dealing with a mosquito problem near your home, contact St. Lucie County mosquito control at 772-462-1962 or email mosquito@stlucieco.org. A 10th-grade student and another person were killed after a multi-vehicle crash involving a school bus happened Monday morning in Central Florida. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news conference that the crash happened around 6 a.m., when a Chevrolet Malibu veered over the center line of a road and hit a Winter Haven High School bus traveling in the opposite direction. There were 37 students on board. The impact of the collision ripped the tire off the bus and caused it to crash head-on into an oncoming Jeep before rolling over off the side of Winter Haven Road. The sheriff said the driver of the Jeep had died. At least five other people involved in the crash were hospitalized, according to authorities. "It was a horrible crash," Judd said. "It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life."The city of Winter Haven is located about 51 miles east of Tampa and 47 miles southwest of Orlando.This story was originally published by Leilyn Torres and Anthony Romano with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

After years of infertility, pregnancy loss and unanswered questions, one Jupiter mother is turning her personal journey into a source of hope for others.The inaugural Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park, bringing together families, wellness providers and community partners with a shared goal: ensuring that no one facing infertility or pregnancy loss feels alone.WATCH: Jupiter woman creates Hope Rising after infertility journeyFor founder Kimberly Malik, the event grew from her own experience navigating five miscarriages and four years of infertility."When you get told unexplained infertility, that's not really what you want to hear and that's not an answer I can accept," Malik said.She spent years researching, advocating for herself and searching for answers before ultimately learning she had a blood-clotting condition that contributed to her losses.Despite the heartbreak, Malik said the experience eventually led her to a larger purpose."Welcomed our rainbow baby on Nov. 8 of 2024, my husband's birthday, and I just felt this calling of don't let others walk alone," she said.That mission became the foundation of Hope Rising.Malik says one of the most difficult parts of infertility and pregnancy loss is the isolation many families experience.The Hope Rising event is designed to change that.Organizers are bringing together local businesses, wellness providers and community partners to create a Support Village where attendees can connect with resources and others who understand the journey firsthand."We can have those that unfortunately are on a fertility journey feel seen and supported," Malik said.Among those helping organize the event is Jenny Frattaruolo, owner of Jupiter Fit Club, who became part of Malik's support system during her fertility journey."Just having resources and having someone along the journey with you is everything," Malik said during an earlier interview.While the event centers around a 5K and fun walk, organizers say the focus extends far beyond race day.Participants will be able to leave messages of encouragement on wooden hearts, honor loved ones through remembrance activities and celebrate children born after pregnancy loss on a Rainbow Baby Wall.The event will also raise money for the Hope Rising Grant, which aims to help Florida families facing the financial challenges often associated with infertility treatment."Fitness is a great way to bring people together, so this race is going to bring a lot of women together and hopefully we can help them find resources," Frattaruolo said.Pregnancy loss remains a topic many families struggle to discuss openly, even though countless people are affected by it.Frattaruolo believes connection can make a meaningful difference."It's one of those, if you know, you know," she said. "I think we will all experience death and grief in our lifetime, but miscarriage is the only death you will experience inside your own body."For Malik, that understanding is exactly why Hope Rising exists.What began as a search for answers has evolved into a movement focused on support, community and hope.The Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park in Jupiter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. — A crown and a lab coat may seem like they belong in two very different worlds, but for Florida Atlantic University graduate student Paige Aldred, they serve the same purpose: getting people to care about the environment around them.Aldred is a biological science master's student at FAU studying water quality, harmful algal blooms, and Sargassum in and around the Indian River Lagoon. She is also Miss Fort Lauderdale, a title she is using to take the science she studies in the lab out into the community.At FAU, Aldred's research examines water quality at locations stretching from Sebastian Inlet south to Jupiter Inlet, including Fort Pierce and the St. Lucie Inlet.“The work that I'm doing at FAU is I'm studying the Indian River Lagoon,” Aldred said. “I'm not only studying the water quality of the Indian River Lagoon, but as well as what the Sargassum is bringing into the Indian River.”For Aldred, much of the work begins with something Floridians know all too well: Sargassum.She collects samples in the field before drying and grinding the seaweed into a fine powder that can be sent for isotope testing. Water associated with the Sargassum is also preserved and analyzed to determine what microscopic organisms may be present.One organism she's investigating is a type of dinoflagellate that has also been detected during research into the unusual spinning behavior observed in fish in the Florida Keys.Aldred is examining whether the organism can travel on Sargassum and make its way into the Indian River Lagoon.“I'm looking to see if that dinoflagellate ... is traveling on Sargassum and finding its way into the Indian River Lagoon,” Aldred said. “And so far I have found traces of that dinoflagellate in my samples.”Researchers are continuing to investigate the cause of the abnormal fish behavior in the Florida Keys, and the presence of a dinoflagellate does not by itself establish that it caused the spinning behavior.Aldred's work doesn't stop when she leaves FAU.As Miss Fort Lauderdale, she uses public appearances and community events to advocate for clean drinking water, healthy ecosystems and more sustainable choices.Aldred said participating in the Miss America organization has also helped her develop another skill she considers important for scientists: communicating complicated research to people outside the scientific community.“Now I have opportunities where I can speak in front of people, but not just speak in front of scientists, speak in front of the community,” Aldred said. “And be able to communicate and translate my science into ways that the community can understand how it impacts them and what they can do to make that difference.”Her environmental message even extends to her pageant wardrobe.Aldred says the clothing she wears for appearances is thrifted, upcycled or purchased secondhand. Rather than continually buying new outfits, she reworks pieces she already owns with different accessories, jackets and styling.The choice is intended to call attention to fast fashion, textile waste and synthetic fibers that can shed from clothing.“We have to understand that we are wearing clothes each day that are shedding,” Aldred said.She encourages people to consider natural fibers, secondhand clothing, upcycled materials and simply asking whether they need to purchase another new item.Aldred also works with children, including through environmental education materials for students in kindergarten through 12th grade.During some classroom visits, she brings trash collected from beaches and places it around the classroom before students enter.When the children question why garbage is in their space, Aldred turns the reaction into a lesson: marine animals are experiencing the same thing when human trash enters their environment.But there's another message she hopes young girls take away when Miss Fort Lauderdale walks into their classroom wearing a crown.“I absolutely love when I go out in the community and, you know, the little girls see a princess,” Aldred said. “But I want them to not only see a princess but a girl who's in science, a girl who can get her hands dirty ... as well as a girl who wants to create that change.”For Aldred, the crown and the science aren't competing identities. One helps her study what's happening in Florida's waters. The other gives her a platform to make sure people understand why it matters.

The man accused of crossing state lines and traveling to Indian River County to kill his ex-girlfriend was booked into the Indian River County Jail on Monday. According to Indian River County Jail records, Matthew Waggle, 33, was booked into the Indian River County Jail at around 5:20 a.m. He faces a charge of first-degree murder. CBS12 reported on the August shooting after authorities found the victim's body, identified as Dawn Kriskewic , in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Investigators say Waggle traveled to Vero Beach by bus and Uber before allegedly killing Kriskewic outside her home Sunday morning. See also: FHP: Wrong-way driver caused deadly I-95 crash Sunday near PB Lakes Boulevard Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said surveillance video captured Waggle walking through Kriskewic's neighborhood shortly after an Uber dropped him off. Investigators say Waggle then left the area, taking an Uber back to Orlando before boarding another Greyhound bus. He eventually made his way to West Virginia, where investigators say he hid at a motel. Flowers said at the time that Flock Safety cameras were instrumental in tracking down Waggle. Authorities had later tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him.

A 17-year-old died after being shot near a boat ramp in Indian River County late Friday night, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the 3700 block of County Road 512, near Garcia's Boat Ramp, at approximately 11:24 p.m. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp The sheriff's office said deputies found the 17-year-old and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. Two women are in custody in Martin County after a shooting at a tow yard led to a police chase and a violent crash Friday afternoon. “I have more questions than I have answers,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek said the incident began around 1 p.m. when two women arrived at Gary’s Towing and Recovery, 4405 SE Cove Road, near Stuart, to retrieve a car that had been towed earlier that morning. While they were there, two other individuals showed up to claim the same vehicle. “They got into some type of argument about the belongings in the car, which, by the way, the only thing in the car really was a couple of guns,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said one of the original women then grabbed a gun and began shooting. No one was injured, but bullets struck trailers in the yard. “It’s just crazy how it went down,” said Gary Reed, the owner of Gary’s Towing and Recovery. Reed, who was not present during the shooting, said his employee called him, screaming for help. And I’m running as fast as I can,” Reed said. https://www.facebook.com/MartinCountySheriffsOffice/posts/pfbid0enPBfuxCWxva9Ce6vmU7hGP3nKdhfidsLzp1e7zxkZ58uSYxB3KhHPTdVi9kagZnl By the time deputies and Reed arrived at the scene, all four individuals involved had fled. The sheriff said the accused shooter had taken the car they were disputing, but deputies located her shortly later on Cove Road near U.S. She attempted to flee but was quickly arrested. Investigators identified her as Jade Rondon, 23, from Miami. The other woman she was with has been identified as Valerie Valdes, 22, also from Miami. Budensiek said she was taken into custody after causing a violent collision on U.S. “Why she was driving at a high rate of speed, why she was weaving out of traffic, we’re not sure. We didn’t even know for sure that that car was involved at that time,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators are working to answer these questions and plan to obtain search warrants for the suspects’ cars and phones. He hopes to have more answers by next week. Rondon already is facing two counts of aggravated assault with a firearm, discharging a firearm in public, aggravated fleeing and eluding, driving while license suspended, felony criminal mischief. Valdes has been cited for operating an unregistered motor vehicle and four counts of reckless driving with injuries. Because the incident was a half-mile from Murray Middle School, MCSO activated an active-shooter response and placed the school on lockout. President Donald Trump rallied supporters at Butler High School in Ohio on Saturday, urging them to consider him as a key factor as he continued his midterm campaign push."We win when I'm on the ballot," Trump said.The rally is part of what Trump calls a 32-day tour ahead of the election to help boost Republicans amid a number of competitive races across the country.RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground statesOhio is home to several closely watched races. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is seeking to unseat incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted in a race that could determine who controls the Senate. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is also running against Democrat Amy Acton."On election night Ohio is going to prove America does not belong to those who hate it, America belongs to those who love it," Trump said.Trump touted both Republican candidates and his administration to the crowd. His message included promoting investments, tariffs and action against Iran, defending data centers — which have divided some Republicans — and promising they would ensure the centers benefit communities, while warning against Democratic leadership.A short distance from the rally, 1,400 people at a Navistar truck factory were laid off, according to the Associated Press.The campaign push comes as polls show persistent voter concerns about the economy. A recent AP/NORC poll found only 17% of adults approved of his handling of the cost of living. More broadly, a number of polls show the president's approval rating generally under 40%.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump claims Iran is waiting until after midterm elections to strike dealTrump dismissed the surveys to the crowd, contending they do not account for his campaigning."They don't account that Trump is out campaigning," he said.He spoke to a high school stadium filled with supporters donning MAGA gear, many touting support for Trump — some for all three campaigns. One protestor was drowned out by the crowd."I think we're gonna have a surprise," Trump said."Just get out and vote and if you do that we're gonna win big," Trump said.Trump has acknowledged concern over messaging and races in some states in recent days. His focus in the final weeks ahead of the election has centered on red states to thank supporters — including Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama — with a visit to Nebraska ahead.

A wrong-way driver sparked a deadly three-vehicle crash early Sunday morning on I-95 in West Palm Beach, killing one person and seriously injuring two others, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP).The crash happened around 5:30 a.m. Sunday on the northbound lanes of I-95 near Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard.Investigators say a GMC Sierra pickup truck was traveling south in the inside lane of northbound I-95, driving the wrong way as it approached Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard. A Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy spotted the vehicle traveling the wrong way and paced it at about 60 to 65 mph before losing sight of it shortly before the crash.A Dodge Grand Caravan was traveling north in the inside lane when its driver, later identified as Angelo Genova, 68, of West Palm Beach, attempted to swerve right to avoid the oncoming pickup but was unable to avoid a collision.Following the initial impact, the pickup rotated and came to rest in the inside northbound lane. The van spun across the roadway from west to east.A Cadillac El Dorado was traveling north behind the van and was unable to avoid the wreckage. The Cadillac then struck the rear of the van, according to FHP.Genova was pronounced dead at the scene.The wrong-way driver, identified in an arrest report as Edwin Castro, 26, of West Palm Beach, and the Cadillac driver suffered serious injuries and were transported to St. Mary's Medical Center for treatment. FHP said the driver of the Cadallic suffered incapacitating injuries. According to the arrest report, deputies and troopers observed that Castro showed signs of impairment after the crash, including a strong odor of alcohol, bloodshot eyes and slurred speech. Hospital toxicology results showed Castro's blood alcohol level was 0.239, nearly three times Florida's legal limit of 0.08, investigators said.Castro was arrested and charged with DUI causing death, vehicular homicide, DUI causing serious bodily injury, reckless driving causing serious bodily injury, two counts of DUI causing property damage or injury and two counts of reckless driving causing property damage or injury. He was also cited for driving the wrong way on the interstate.The arrest report also states that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement told investigators that Castro had a final order of removal after a denied asylum claim from Guatemala.All northbound lanes of I-95 at Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard remained closed while the crash was being investigated but have since reopened.

By: Emma Romano Posted and last updated PALM BEACH, Fla. — A female manatee that washed ashore in Palm Beach Saturday morning has safely returned to the ocean, authorities said. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and West Palm Beach police responded after the manatee was found out of the water. Officials at the scene said the female manatee came ashore while trying to get away from male manatees attempting to mate with her. FWC and police remained at the scene and monitored the manatee while waiting for her to return to the water on her own. The manatee eventually made her way off the beach and back into the ocean.

A 17-year-old boy died after a shooting late Friday close to a boat ramp near Fellsmere and Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Saturday. The Indian River School District said the unnamed teen recently withdrew from Sebastian River High School to homeschool and was not enrolled in the district at the time of the shooting. "We are deeply saddened by the loss of this young person, and our hearts are with his family, friends, and the Sebastian River High School community," district spokeswoman Kyra Schafte said in a statement to WPBF. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

WPTV learned there are 13 license plate reader cameras in St. Lucie County that don't have permits, according to county staff.Wednesday, Sept. 30, was the deadline the Florida Department of Transportation gave municipalities to remove the license plate readers from state-controlled roads.WATCH BELOW: Unpermitted license plate readers found in St. Lucie CountyNow WPTV is pressing city leaders about why the cameras are there, who they belong to, and what is happening to the cameras now.On Thursday, WPTV spoke to Ricky Mathura, who works at a gas station off Orange Avenue and 25th Street in Fort Pierce, where one of the unpermitted license plate readers was found."I don't know why it's there," said Mathura. Lucie County Communications Director Erick Gill said they're trying to find that out."We don't know who they belong to," Gill said. "They were just put in our right-of-way."The county says there's 53 permitted license plate readers on their right-of-ways and gave WPTV a list with all the locations of the unpermitted license plate readers staff found.RELATED: FDOT revokes permits for automated license plate readers"We were surprised, you know, that were that many out there,” said Gill.The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office told WPTV they claimed three of them but are working to find out why they weren't permitted.Gill said county staff is actively working to identify the owners of the other readers and taped notices on the cameras for the owners to take them down within 30 days.Once the 30 days are up, Gill said staff will remove the readers safely."We'll begin the process of either removing them if we feel like we can safely remove them without damaging the equipment and endangering our staff, or at least covering up so the cameras can't capture any surveillance," Gill said.

A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community.The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million.The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. “That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women,” said Pietrewicz.After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on.“We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately,” she said.WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it.The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors.“You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals,” said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging.Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location.But some seniors say the location itself is important.“That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community,” Pietrewicz said.Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live.“We live here, we want rights to do thing, besides trouble,” Lovett said.The Council on Aging said it understands those concerns, but says change is necessary.For now, the Council on Aging says services at the Orange Avenue center are continuing. There is no finalized timeline for the closure because the transition is tied to the sale of the property.“We understand the concerns, it's a change for us too. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change,” Smith said.The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St.

WPTV is looking into drainage and septic issues on the Treasure Coast. Neighbor Daniel Fletchall reached out to our news team about septic issues in his community on Northwest Sunset Boulevard in Jensen Beach. WATCH BELOW: 'I'm forced to live in this filth': Neighbors demand septic solution Fletchall said after a heavy rain, he and his neighbors' septic backs up and comes up into their yards "The sewage water from the septic tank will actually make its way up out of the tank and into my yard," said Fletchall. "It smells back here, and I can't let my dog out." Fletchall said they can't even flush their toilets for days. "I got to go down to Home Depot or go to the mall to use the bathroom," said Fletchall. Fletchall added he can't shower or wash his clothes. "Thankfully, my parents live nearby, so I can go take a shower," said Fletchall. "But it's just not happening here.” Fletchall isn't the only one affected by this issue. Neighbors like Christie Berger are also having septic issues every time there's heavy rain. "I go to McDonald's to use the bathroom if I have to," Berger said. Neighbor Rachelle Kukan said it's becoming unacceptable. "I wish I could just kind of pick up and move because this is such a problem and it's so serious to me that I would leave if I could," said Kukan. Fletchall said he had septic companies come out to fix the drainage in his yard. Elevating the septic tank, Fletchall said, would be costly, and even then he's been told it might not solve the problem. Fletchall said he'd like the Martin County staff to extend the sewer lines into his neighborhood. "I'm forced to live in this filth, and I still pay the taxes every year to have things done around the county, but I’m not getting any help here," said Fletchall. WPTV reached out to Martin County about any solutions. Staff said the neighborhood on Northwest Sunset Boulevard is on the list to get septic-to-sewer conversions, but no date has been set yet. Staff said they're looking at ways to potentially move the neighborhood up on the list of systems to convert.

Two women are under arrest after a shooting at Garry's Towing and Recovery in Martin County triggered a school lockout, a police chase and a separate crash. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says more charges could be coming.Jade Rondon, a Miami resident, opened fire in the tow yard on Southeast Cove Road shortly after 1 p.m.WATCH BELOW: Tow yard shooting leads to arrests; more charges possibleThe sheriff's office says the car she came to retrieve had been involved in criminal activity Thursday evening, then reported stolen. Detectives recovered it Friday morning.Around 1 p.m., Rondon arrived at the tow yard accompanied by another woman, Valerie Valdes. Shortly after, individuals in another car arrived at the facility, and the two parties became involved in an altercation, deputies said."They got into some type of argument about the belongings in the car which by the way the only thing really in the car was a couple guns," Sheriff John Budensiek said.Rondon got a gun and fired multiple shots at the other individuals before getting into the car and leaving the area. The individuals who were shot at also left the scene before deputies arrived.Garry Reed, the owner of Garry's Towing and Recovery, said his employee was left shaken by the ordeal."Young lady who works in my office — she was terrorized," Reed said.Reed told me they had helped the Martin County Sheriff's Office recover the car Friday morning, but when the owner came to pick it up this afternoon, things turned dangerous."The young lady went to see what was going on and all of a sudden she heard gunfire," Reed said."[It’s] scary. I'm racing — my heart is racing," Reed said.Because the tow yard is located near Murray Middle School, the sheriff's office immediately activated an active-shooter response and placed the school on lockout.Road patrol deputies, aviation, detectives and other available units quickly began searching for Rondon's car and located it traveling on Cove Road near US-1. Deputies attempted a traffic stop, but she fled, forcing deputies to perform a PIT maneuver to bring the car to a stop.Later, Valdes was reportedly driving recklessly, lost control and caused a significant crash near Osprey Street and US-1. No one was seriously hurt.The Sheriff's Office is still conducting search warrants and reviewing data and video evidence to figure out what happened at the tow yard."We're honestly not sure what we have," Budensiek said. "We're sure that shots are fired. We're sure that she fled from our deputies. Something happened with that vehicle the night before. There was a reason why everyone had interest in that car."Rondon faces two counts of aggravated assault with a firearm, discharging a firearm in public, aggravated fleeing and eluding, driving with a suspended license and felony criminal mischief. Valdes faces charges for operating an unregistered motor vehicle and four counts of reckless driving with injuries. The sheriff says more charges are likely as investigators piece together what happened.Despite the chaos, Reed said he is counting his blessings."Thank God that everybody was okay," Reed said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

In April, he was named Florida Youth of the Year. Two months later, he earned the title of Southeast Youth of the Year, advancing to the national level of competition.In July, Rosario Liz received another surprise when the Boys & Girls Clubs of America selected him to attend the FIFA World Cup final as a flag bearer.
