Coco Gauff came back to defeat Ons Jabeur 4-6, 6-2, 6-3 at the French Open on Tuesday to reach the semifinals at a third consecutive Grand Slam tournament.Gauff won her first major title at the U.S. Open in September, then made it to the final four at the Australian Open in January.The 20-year-old American is seeded No. 3 at Roland Garros, where she was the runner-up to Iga Swiatek in 2022.Gauff could get a rematch in the semifinals against the top-ranked Swiatek, who has won three of the past four titles in Paris.Swiatek’s quarterfinal against 2023 Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova was scheduled for later Tuesday on Court Philippe Chatrier.Jabeur's mix of speeds and spins gave Gauff fits at times. And as well-known as Gauff is for her ability to cover the court and play defense, Jabeur managed to keep coming up with winners, finishing with 30 in all.“She was playing really well the whole match. She was hitting a lot of winners on me, which is something I’m not used to against anybody,” Gauff said. “So today I was just trying to just be aggressive toward the end.”Gauff pulled away to a 5-2 lead in the last set, then needed a trio of match points to close things out, acknowledging afterward that maybe she grew a little tight down the stretch. The last game was key, with Gauff needing to save a break point, then Jabeur dismissing one match point with a disguised drop shot that earned a roar from the stands that the 29-year-old Tunisian responded to by putting her right index finger to her ear.But on Gauff's next opportunity to seal the victory, Jabeur badly flubbed an overhead. Gauff smiled, then raised her arms and yelled.With the crowd at the main stadium loudly supporting Jabeur at times, Gauff did not play badly in the opening set. 8 seed Jabeur — a three-time major finalist — was superb, winning 17 of 18 first-serve points, never facing a single break point and accumulating a 12-5 edge in total winners.When she delivered an ace at 114 mph (184 kph) to end the set, Jabeur nodded repeatedly.“She’s a tough opponent and she’s well-loved on tour. I could tell by the crowd today — I know you guys wanted her to win. Honestly, whenever she’s not playing (me), I cheer for her, too,” Gauff said.“Even though you guys were for Ons, I really had a lot of fun, even when I lost the first set and they were chanting when I was in the bathroom," Gauff said about her trip off the court after the first set. "I was like, ‘This is just really fun, win or lose.’ It is.”Gauff got going after that, raising her level and trying to gain the upper hand during lengthier exchanges. She put in 16 winners over the last two sets, while breaking serve four times.“I know I have a lot of love here in Paris. Trust me, I know," said Gauff, who won the French Open junior title at age 14. "So I really appreciate it, and hopefully you guys can help me make it through the next round.”

The criminal charges against world No. 1 golfer Scottie Scheffler have been dismissed following his arrest earlier this month at the PGA Championship in Louisville, Kentucky."Based upon the totality of the evidence, my office cannot move forward in the prosecution of the charges filed against Mr. Scheffler," Jefferson County Attorney Mike O'Connell said at a brief hearing Wednesday. Scheffler's actions and the evidence surrounding their exchange during the misunderstanding do not satisfy the elements of any criminal offenses," O'Connell added. The judge then accepted his motion to have the charges dismissed.Scheffler, 27, was taken into custody by Louisville Police on May 17 outside Valhalla Golf Club ahead of the second round of the tournament. He was booked on four criminal counts, including assault of a police officer, criminal mischief, reckless driving and disregarding signals from officers directing traffic.A police report obtained by Scripps News says he attempted to drive around traffic that was caused by a fatal accident near the country club. The report says Scheffler "refused to comply" with an officer directing traffic and "accelerated forward, dragging Detective Gillis to the ground."The officer was reportedly transported to a nearby hospital to be examined for "pain, swelling and abrasions to his left wrist and knee."Surveillance footage released by Louisville police last week appeared to show Gillis approaching Scheffler's vehicle on foot before stopping him from entering the golf course. Scheffler can later be seen being led away in handcuffs.In a statement released by the PGA Tour following his arrest, Scheffler described the incident as a "big misunderstanding.""I was proceeding as directed by police officers," he said. "It was a very chaotic situation, understandably so considering the tragic accident that had occurred earlier, and there was a big misunderstanding of what I thought I was being asked to do. I never intended to disregard any of the instructions."Louisville police said last week they were looking into whether officers violated any department policies during the arrest. Gillis has since been disciplined for not having his body camera activated at the time of the incident.

Health authorities in France are sounding the alarm as cases of dengue continue to rise ahead of the 2024 Olympic Games.Officials say that this year alone there have been about “1,649 imported cases,” compared to about 131 cases reported around the same time last year, according to Euronews.The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says that the bulk of these cases stem from Guadeloupe and Martinique, where an "epidemic" is currently underway, as French Guiana has reported 7,000 confirmed dengue cases since the beginning of 2024.Officials are concerned because the Paris 2024 Olympic Games are only a few months away and scheduled to start on July 26, 2024.However, the French are not the only ones affected. This year, over 5 million cases have been reported worldwide that have resulted in 2,000 deaths, the ECDPC reports.The World Health Organization says that most of these cases are coming from the Americas, with Brazil, Argentina and Puerto Rico leading in cases.In March, Puerto Rico declared a public health emergency as the island reported 549 cases, nearly half of the total for the entire year of 2023 (1,242 cases). As of its latest data from April, the number had risen to 795.Dengue is a disease spread by mosquito bites, and symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pains, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands, rash, difficulty breathing, fatigue, and eye pain. If you have any of these symptoms, officials say to contact your primary care physician.

Palm Beach Gardens police have launched an investigation into professional golfer Grayson Murray's death. Police said Murray's body was found in a home at approximately 11 a.m. Just one day prior, Murray had withdrawn from the Charles Schwab Challenge, citing an illness.Murray's parents confirmed to the PGA Tour that the 30-year-old "took his own life."The initial investigation did not reveal any signs of foul play, Palm Beach Gardens police said.Police added that no further information will be released during the investigation.The 30-year-old golfer won three consecutive Callaway Junior World Championships and became the top-ranked golfer in his age group. When Murray was 16, he made the first cut on the Korn Ferry Tour, and became the second-youngest player to achieve the victory.Murray would later go on to Wake Forest University, East Carolina University, and Arizona State University, before he got his break in 2016 gaining a sponsor’s exemption into the Korn Ferry Tour near Raleigh, North Carolina — his hometown — the PGA Tour said.Murray was able to earn full status on the PGA Tour for the 2016-2017 season.

Rapper Pitbull has scored the naming rights to Florida International University’s football stadium in a new partnership with the Miami school.As part of a 10-year agreement, the university’s FIU Stadium will be rebranded as Pitbull Stadium, making it the first athletics stadium to be named after an artistPitbull, also known as “Mr. 305” for his Miami roots, will donate $1.2 million each year for the next five years as part of the deal.In addition to naming rights, Pitbull will be able to host up to 10 events a year, including concerts, at Pitbull Stadium. The school’s online store also has FIU x Pitbull merchandise available for purchase.The rapper, known for hits like "I Know You Want Me (Calle Ocho)," spoke out about the announcement."This partnership with FIU is a true honor and a testament to what we can achieve when we work hard," the music artist said in a press release. "Renaming the stadium isn't just about a name change. It's about inspiring the community, creating opportunities and showing the world that with determination and a clear vision, anything is possible. We're making history together, and we're just getting started. Why dream when you can live it?"FIU’s athletics director Scott Carr also commented on the partnership with the rapper, whose full name is Armando Christian Perez."This is a historic day for FIU Athletics to uniquely partner with a world-renowned artist and amazing person who truly values relationships and his community," Carr said in a press release. "Armando's financial support is program-changing, but him providing a microphone to amplify FIU will be even more beneficial to growing our brand. I couldn't be more excited about our partnership as this will take us to another level. We can now officially say: 'Paws Up, Dale!'"Van Wagner College, a third-party multimedia rights partner with FIU Athletics since 2016, assisted in the deal. The school helped secure additional partners, such as South Dade Kia, which FIU said will be the presenting sponsor of the field — South Dade Kia Field at Pitbull Stadium.No stranger to the education space, Pitbull also founded the first tuition-free public charter SLAM! school — for sports leadership, arts and management — in Miami in 2012.

West Palm Beach native Markus Edegran is ready and hopeful to compete in his first Olympics.Markus will be competing in kite foiling. This combines kite boarding and foiling. Foiling is the latest technique to come into sailing.A foil is a type of board with an extended rudder. This allows the board to rise above the water and the sailor to move at much faster paces without the friction of the water along the board.When you achieve foiling, it is almost like you are flying over the water. Although it looks serene and peaceful, it is very difficult to achieve.Markus told us that it takes a lot of patience and balance to maintain the necessary foiling technique. He also explained that kite foiling goes at extreme paces, about 50 mph across the waters. He explained it best when he said that he can kite foil from Lake Worth Beach to the Juno Beach Pier faster than we can drive it.Markus explained to us what foiling means for the sport of sailing."The foiling is the way the sport is heading," Markus said. It's more exciting to sail. It's more exciting to watch. I think that half the classes are foiling classes. So yeah, super excited to be a part of that."He had an early introduction to the water as he followed his brothers’ footsteps and started sailing at 8 years old. He said there was a steep learning curve, but he was automatically hooked.I asked him about his emotions ahead of the games and he didn’t have much to say regarding those. Markus is very calm ahead of the games and is treating it just like any other five-day race."I'm super happy it all lined up and brought me here today," Markus said.He has been training in the Marseille waters off and on for the last three years ahead of the games. We are rooting for you Markus and hope you contribute to the USA medal count.Markus’ competition begins on Aug.

Boca Raton native Caroline Marks from the United States won the women's surfing gold medal on Monday at the Paris Olympics in Tahiti, while French Polynesian Kauli Vaast won the gold medal in men’s surfing.Marks, 22, was born in Boca but grew up in Melbourne Beach in Brevard County.SPECIAL COVERAGE: 2024 Paris OlympicsCheers and tears erupted from boats floating near the wave and crowds of spectators along the shore as the men's final match ended in the afternoon. Vaast pumped his arms into the air in victory after beating Jack Robinson from Australia, who received the silver medal.“I don’t really realize it, but I just made history,” said Vaast. “I can’t be prouder to represent Tahiti and France at home.”The women's gold medal match ended about thirty minutes later, with Marks beating Tatiana Weston-Webb from Brazil, who was awarded the silver medal.“Your whole life goes into a moment like this,” Marks said with a gold medal hanging around her neck. “It’s beyond all my wildest dreams.”For the bronze medals, Gabriel Medina from Brazil and Johanne Defay from France won after beating Alonso Correa from Peru and Brisa Hennessy from Costa Rica, respectively.“Chopes gave me so many good waves, so many good results. So I can’t complain,” said Medina, using a common nickname for Teahupo'o.Medalists — some in bare feet — stepped on to the Olympic podium near the ocean as crowds gathered to cheer and take photographs. Roosters ran along the grass while young local surfers called the names of the athletes as they walked by.All winners of the Paris Olympics surfing competition are first-time Olympic medalists, after defending Olympic women’s champion Carissa Moore of the United States — who won at the Tokyo Games, where Olympic surfing debuted — was beaten in the quarterfinals on Thursday.“Obviously I’m really sad to not be a part of finals day, to get to represent my home and my family one more time, but I’m really grateful,” Moore said after her loss. “I just hope that at the end of the day I can encourage whoever is watching, win or lose, don’t be afraid to go into it fearlessly and don’t be afraid to fail.”The final day of the Paris Olympics surfing competition began Monday morning after two days of delays due to unfavorable conditions. In the morning, conditions were smaller than the heavy, barrel-shaped waves Teahupo’o is famed for and that were seen during part of the men’s competition the week before.But by the afternoon waves grew larger and more frequent, giving athletes a chance to impress judges with the time they spent inside the barrels. At one point during the competition a whale jumped out of the water while surfers went head to head.Six of the eight surfers who made it to the semifinals represented different nations. French Polynesian, Peruvian, Australian and other national flags flew from boats near the waves.While not every surfer who competed was able to bring home a medal, many agreed that the second-ever Olympics surfing competition — filled with viral photographs, record-breaking scores and hours of stunning video footage broadcast to viewers around the world — helped promote the sport."Everyone’s watching and paying attention,” said Medina, who said he gained millions of social media followers after a photo of him floating in the sky next to his surfboard while bailing out of a wave went viral during the competition.

Gustav Forsling hammered a shot past Brandon Bussi with 4.3 seconds left in overtime to lift the Florida Panthers past the reigning Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes 1-0 in Tuesday's season opener for both teams.On a night when the defenses and goaltenders had the edge, it was a blue-liner who provided the winning play to end a matchup of the last two teams to win the Cup.The Panthers had their final chance with the game seemingly headed to a shootout as Carter Verhaeghe brought the puck into the zone with under 10 seconds left. But Verhaeghe sent the puck back toward Forsling, who fired a one-timer from near the blue line that zipped past Bussi's glove side to end it.That spoiled the end of a three-month celebration for the Hurricanes since beating Vegas in June to cap a 16-3 march to the franchise's second Cup. The final piece was the players gathering at the blue line and tapping their sticks as a championship banner rose to the rafters.That moment came against the Panthers, who reached the Stanley Cup Final for three straight years and won it all in 2024 and 2025. They had twice eliminated the Hurricanes in the Eastern Conference Final in their run, though injuries derailed last year.Getting captain Aleksander Barkov back from that lengthy injury list was one of several reasons to expect the Panthers to jump right back into contention, along with Panthers star Matthew Tkachuk welcoming brother Brady as an offseason addition. There was also the change by bringing in Jacob Markstrom to take over the crease anchored by Sergei Bobrovsky during those title runs.And for much of this one, it was up to Markstrom and Bussi to hold up in net, including against multiple one-on-one quality chances and a combined 13 power plays in regulation.Markstrom finished with 15 saves while Bussi — who posted a shutout in Carolina's Cup-clinching win against Vegas — made 19 saves before giving up the last blast.Panthers: Florida heads west to face the San Jose Sharks on Thursday.Hurricanes: Carolina hosts the Washington Capitals on Friday night.

Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

Outrage and frustration boiled over at a community meeting in Indiantown, as residents packed a room to demand answers from the Martin County Sheriff's Office after a parent who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop was not charged with a crime.The tense Monday night meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and the sheriff, centered on the sheriff's determination that the father acted in self-defense. However, many residents argued that the man should have been arrested for the separate crime of possessing a firearm at a school bus stop.WATCH BELOW: Indiantown divided over bus stop gun incident, no-charge decisionSheriff John Budensiek laid out his office's account of the incident, which occurred just over a week ago. He said it began with a student being bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver.The situation escalated, Budensiek said, when the alleged bully and a friend "pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the dad.""He puts his hand up and backs up, backs up, says 'stay away, stay away,' and they don't," Budensiek explained. "In fact, they’re yelling that they’re going to whoop his hind end... He pulls out a gun and all of a sudden they’re backing up, because they don’t want to get shot."The sheriff defended the lack of charges against the father, citing the state's self-defense laws. "In the state of Florida, you’re allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," he said.But residents at the meeting were furious, arguing that the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his "Stand Your Ground" defense."Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled.The sheriff countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a "bus stop," making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father also declined to press battery charges against the two students.Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws."These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket."He said that while there was disagreement, everyone shared one sentiment: "We can agree that this should have never happened."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. In doing so, the defendant made sure that the city-owned land would ultimately be leased by LPYP and no one else," Bridges said.LPYP stands for the Lincoln Park Young Professionals, the local nonprofit involved in the case.The defense countered that Mimms showed no favoritism, and that a $500,000 grant provided by the Alleghany Franciscan Ministries toward the development of the site in Lincoln Park did not involve the city."They started work on the project, and it failed, and that's the sad truth. Days after raising speculation about her 2028 prospects in a New York Times interview, U.S. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said she is focused on helping Democrats — including herself — win reelection in 2026.Ocasio-Cortez has recently been the subject of speculation about a possible 2028 Democratic presidential bid, a race expected to draw a crowded field. Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party's chances in November.A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the Republican president's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.A majority, 65%, of U.S. adults now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control, signaling growing weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and continued unhappiness with the war with Iran.The dismal numbers come just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress and while Trump is hitting the campaign trail with an aggressive schedule of rallies. But Trump — who has asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot as he tries to bolster turnout — remains deeply unpopular, with even many Republicans faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.RELATED STORY | Fed raises rates despite pressure from Trump to cut borrowing costs“I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good," said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Bradford, Pennsylvania, who describes himself as a Republican.“Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. He’s not really done what I was hoping he would," said Gault. "He said, 'Make America Great Again.' And I have not seen him do that.”Costs drag on Trump as the economic pain keeps comingOver the last few months, Americans have grown more worried about being able to afford basics like groceries and gas. adults now say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July. About half are also highly concerned about being able to afford food.Prices are "extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel,” said Pedro Sanchez, 52, of Perris, California, who voted for Trump and works in law enforcement. “I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more. It’s gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.”Trump’s current approval on the economy is a 14 percentage point drop from March 2025, just after he took office for the second time. His struggles on the issue mark a significant departure from his first term, when the economy was often a point of strength.Trump spent much of the 2024 campaign hammering President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats, on inflation and promising to lower prices. Now, there's widespread disappointment with his performance. About 7 in 10 Americans say Trump’s handling of the cost of living has been “worse than expected." That includes roughly half of Republicans, who are also broadly concerned about being able to afford groceries and gas.“Groceries are just like kind of out of control. It seems like everything is going up," said Bethany Lnenicka, 41, who operates a small farm in Fairfax, Iowa. “It's just one thing and the next week it's another thing. And of course your income doesn’t go up.”A political independent who typically votes Republican and has voted for Trump three times, Lnenicka said she had hoped his second term would be more like his first.“I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better," she said.About 6 in 10 Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, according to the new poll, up from about half in April.“It definitely doesn’t feel like we have trended in the right direction," agreed Kristen Slaven, 41, a mental health therapist who lives in Gluckstadt, Mississippi, and typically votes Republican. She said Trump is focused on the wrong things.“Obviously wars don’t help. When they’re necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that’s just stupid to me when people can't feed their family," she said.RELATED STORY | Trump is on tour touting the economy, but Americans seem to be losing confidence in the message“I had hoped that it would be better,” Slaven added.Some Republicans are still willing to cut Trump some slackDespite their frustration, most Republicans, 67%, say factors outside of Trump's control are more to blame for high prices.“I think inflation is a very difficult thing to tackle," said Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter who lives in Green Bay, Wisconsin.Though he would like to see interest rates come down, Naumann, who works in the automotive industry, supports tariffs and the war with Iran, believing it was necessary.Overall, however, most Americans, 69%, continue to say the war has not been worth fighting, up slightly from 64% in July. Only 28% approve of how Trump is handling Iran.Americans are also unhappy with Trump's trade wars. adults approve of how he is handling trade negotiations with other countries, down from about 4 in 10 in March. And 64% say he has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries, up from 58% in January.Overall, the picture is not better. Only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling his job as president. And about 6 in 10 say the country as a whole is “much” or “somewhat” worse off than when he began his second term.The issue on which Trump maintains relative strength is border security, with about half of Americans saying they approve of his performance.Trump faces more blame than Biden didTrump's low grade on the economy rivals Biden’s 28% approval rating in June 2022, when there was record-high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic.But Americans were less likely to blame Biden in the lead-up to that year's midterm elections, a sharp contrast with the solid majority who hold Trump responsible now. In October 2022, 44% of Americans said Biden’s policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside of his control.Sanchez, a Republican who voted for Trump, blames him, at least in part.“I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he’s placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us. Those two things are things he’s been directly involved in that directly affect the economy,” he said. “I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control. It was all the COVID and how that affected everything else. I don’t think that there was much that he could have done."He had high hopes for Trump's return. Now, things seem worse than under Biden.

Posted Gas prices are reshaping the political landscape in Peachtree City, Georgia, a Fayette County community that has backed Republicans for decades but that Democrats believe they can flip in the upcoming midterms. With prices approaching $5 a gallon, some longtime Trump supporters say their loyalty is wavering. First-time voter Charlotte Willis says the prices finally pushed her to register. Gas prices are weighing heavily on voters all over the country, and that is true in Peachtree City, Georgia. When asked if he voted for Trump in the last election, Manetti confirmed he did — and said he is now potentially considering voting Democrat.Gas pump frustration is also creating new voters. "I never had voted," Willis told the Scripps News Group's Joe St. "And you are going to vote in this election?" St. "And I guess you're going to vote Democrat?" St. George spoke with voters sits in a part of Georgia that has backed Republicans for decades. Tens of thousands of Boy Scout sexual abuse survivors are still waiting for payment from a billion-dollar settlement, while nearly $40 million has already gone to trustee and legal fees since the trust fund was approved three years ago.Lee Forbes, Curtis Garrison and Kenneth Richter are among the more than 62,000 survivors who have been approved for settlements through the Boy Scouts of America bankruptcy trust.Watch full report from I-Team Investigative reporter Katie LaGroneFor Forbes, the settlement represents justice for abuse, he said, that lasted nearly two years while he was a teen scout in the Explorer program. "It's all the justice I'm going to get," he said.For Garrison, the money represents accountability."They need to pay us in full for all the harm they've done," he said.Our recent investigation found that five years after the Boy Scouts agreed to settle one of the costliest child sex abuse cases in U.S. history, its bankruptcy trust fund does not have enough money to pay all 62,000 survivors what they are owed. With less than five weeks until Election Day, a campaign ad from Republican Byron Donalds claims Democrat David Jolly's hurricane insurance proposal would cost Florida families $1,000 a year in what the ad calls a "hurricane tax." An examination of the ad and the study it cites tells a more complicated story.The Donalds ad's claimsThe ad opens by asking, "How much will David Jolly's hurricane tax cost Florida?" and cites a Florida State University study to support its assertion that Jolly's plan would run Florida families $1,000 per year."A giant bail-out for big insurance. A giant rip-off for you," the 30-second spot says.WATCH BELOW: Fact-check: Hurricane insurance ad claim examinedRELATED: More political, election newsWhat Jolly is proposingJolly wants to create what he calls a "sovereign wealth fund" to absorb all windstorm coverage in Florida, while allowing private insurers to handle other types of policies.When I asked him at an event in Fort Lauderdale recently to explain the concept, Jolly pushed back on the "hurricane tax" framing."Well, there's currently a thousand-dollar hurricane tax on the books that Byron Donalds wants to continue. My model would actually repeal it," Jolly said.What's actually on the booksFlorida does not have a specific "hurricane tax" on the books. Jolly is likely referring to the assessments that Citizens Property Insurance is required to levy on Floridians in order to remain solvent.Jolly's campaign claims that if private insurers don't have to worry about windstorm policies, premiums would drop 60 to 70 percent. I was not able to independently verify that math."A state sovereign wealth fund can absorb the risk of hurricane coverage if we sufficiently capitalize it," Jolly said.What the cited FSU study actually saysThe Donalds ad cites a Florida State University study — which I obtained via a public records request. It was commissioned by the policy research arm of the Florida Legislature and released in August.The 80-page report does not examine Jolly's specific proposal of a sovereign wealth fund. Instead, it looks into the feasibility of having Citizens Property Insurance bear all the risk for named windstorms, taking the burden off private insurers.The report says that proposal could — under some circumstances — lower premiums. But it would ultimately redistribute the risk from Florida's most hurricane-prone areas and spread it across the state, "effectively (creating) a broader 'hurricane tax...'" by "(increasing) the likelihood and magnitude of statewide assessments."Read the full study below:How Jolly would fund the sovereign wealth fundI followed up with Jolly, asking how he would get the money for the sovereign wealth fund, which he says would need at least $32 million to start."So let's start with the existing hurricane fund, the $12 billion in the current fee structure," Jolly said. "(And) if we require our insurance companies to actually keep their profits in state instead of shipping them out of state, you could raise several billion dollars a year doing that as well. I've also mentioned looking at a tourist development tax."Jolly also suggested starting with partial windstorm coverage from the fund, then rolling out full coverage as it grows over time.Donalds pushes backDonalds says his opponent's math still doesn't add up."When it comes to insurance company profits, he says he wants to tax, if you take 70% of their business away from them, what profits are you taxing?" Donalds said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The sheriff said one of the original women then grabbed a gun and began shooting. No one was injured, but bullets struck trailers in the yard. “It’s just crazy how it went down,” said Gary Reed, the owner of Gary’s Towing and Recovery. Reed, who was not present during the shooting, said his employee called him, screaming for help. And I’m running as fast as I can,” Reed said. https://www.facebook.com/MartinCountySheriffsOffice/posts/pfbid0enPBfuxCWxva9Ce6vmU7hGP3nKdhfidsLzp1e7zxkZ58uSYxB3KhHPTdVi9kagZnl By the time deputies and Reed arrived at the scene, all four individuals involved had fled. A second woman has been arrested following a chaotic chain of events that began with a shooting at a Martin County tow yard, triggered a nearby school lockout and ended with multiple crashes and a police pursuit. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the incident unfolded shortly after 1 p.m. Friday at Gary's Towing and Recovery on Southeast Cove Road. 23-year-old Jade Ely Rondon, of Miami, arrived at the tow yard to retrieve a BMW that had been towed earlier in the day. Deputies said another group arrived shortly afterward, leading to an altercation. According to the sheriff's office, Rondon retrieved a firearm and fired multiple shots at the other individuals before fleeing the scene in a vehicle. Because the business is located about a half-mile from Murray Middle School, deputies activated an active-shooter response and placed the school on lockout while officers searched for the suspect. Deputies later located Rondon's vehicle near U.S. 1 and attempted a traffic stop. Investigators said she refused to stop, prompting deputies to perform a PIT maneuver and take her into custody. Rondon was arrested and charged with two counts of aggravated assault with firearm, discharging a firearm in public, aggravated fleeing and eluding, driving while license suspended, and felony criminal mischief. See also: Woman arrested at Mar-a-Lago after claiming Sen. Tom Cotton invited her According to the sheriff's office, Valerie Valdes, 24, had accompanied Rondon to the tow yard to retrieve the BMW. After the shooting, deputies said Valdes fled in the vehicle they originally arrived in. "The other female was driving erratically, passing cars, and ended up losing control, going over into the oncoming lane down U.S. 1 and having a significant crash," sheriff John Budensiek said. Investigators said Valdes ultimately crashed at the intersection of Constitutional Boulevard and U.S. She was taken to Cleveland Clinic Martin South Hospital for treatment of her injuries before being arrested. Valdes is charged with operating an unregistered motor vehicle, and four counts of reckless driving with injuries. The people who were allegedly targeted by the gunfire left the towing facility before deputies arrived. CBS12 News spoke with Gary Reed, owner of Gary's Towing and Recovery, who said he's grateful no one at the business was injured. I love all the people around me. Even the people next door," Reed said. Murray Middle School sent out the following message to families: "Good afternoon, Lions! Please note that we have heavy police presence in the area for an incident unrelated to Murray. We are following Martin County Sheriff's Office guidance and are on a lock out. We will remain in close contact with them and provide additional information as it becomes available. Thank you, Principal Roth" The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active and additional charges are possible.

Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to repair a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and recent rain continue to affect parts of South Florida. Skid loaders were working along the narrow roadway beside the Indian River Lagoon, adding dirt and sand to reinforce an area where erosion has left the road’s edge vulnerable. Crews brought 32 loads of dirt to the site Sept. But only days later, the embankment again needed repairs. Resident Gene Barnes said the recurring work is not a long-term solution. We’re losing ground year by year, Barnes said. Until the Corps of Engineers or something like that comes and puts a headwall in to stabilize it, it’s not going to be an easy fix. The road has faced erosion problems before. Heavy rain damaged sections in 2014, and Hurricane Nicole caused additional washouts in 2022. Barnes said continued rain and tidal action could undermine the roadway itself. See also: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge If we keep getting rains like this, it’s going to undermine the road, and then the road is going to collapse and the school bus is going to fall in the hole, he said. The latest repairs follow an emergency sand operation at nearby Jetty Park that cost taxpayers nearly $500,000. While repairs on South Indian River Drive may be less costly, residents said the erosion is likely to remain a concern as more rain and tidal action are forecast.

Eight months after a Port St. Lucie father vanished, his family says they are still searching for answers and living with the painful uncertainty of not knowing where he is. "I'm stuck in this cycle of not knowing where he is," said Aubrey Finley, whose brother, Robert La Polla , disappeared Jan. 8 after being released from a hospital in Fort Pierce. The 47-year-old father has not been seen or heard from since, according to his family. Detectives have no confirmed sightings, and the case remains unsolved. Finley said La Polla struggled with depression following the deaths of their parents, but the siblings remained close and talked often. "Everything kind of fell apart," she said. "But we still managed to communicate a lot. We were still there for each other all the time." Because of that bond, Finley said her brother's disappearance is completely out of character. In the months since he vanished, family members and friends have organized search efforts across Fort Pierce, checking wooded areas and busy corridors near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. "We've gone through woods, under bridges, talking to people everywhere in Fort Pierce, trying to find anything that brings us to him," Finley said. The search has also taken an emotional toll on La Polla's young daughter, who continues to wait for her father to come home. She misses him," Finley said. "He's got a family that love him." The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office (SLCSO) said La Polla has been entered into a national missing persons database. Investigators have also collected DNA from family members in case it is needed for identification and continue to follow up on leads. Anyone with information about La Polla's whereabouts is asked to contact Detective Cpl. Drawdy at 772-462-3230 or call 911.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance both hit the campaign trail on Thursday, but headed to heavily Republican areas to shore up lagging enthusiasm in their party ahead of next month’s midterm elections.Trump’s travel to Texas and Oklahoma kicked off what the president said will be a 32-day campaign blitz leading up to Nov. 3.“I think we’re going to win. A shooting at a tow yard Friday afternoon near a middle school in Martin County triggered a lockout and led to a chase and a Miami woman in custody. The woman opened fire at a tow yard on Southeast Cove Road shortly after 1 p.m., the Martin County Sheriff’s Office said. According to deputies, the woman arrived at the towing facility to claim a car that had been towed there earlier in the day. Shortly after, individuals in another car arrived at the facility, and the two parties became involved in an altercation, deputies said. The woman got a gun and fired multiple shots at the other individuals before getting into a car and leaving the area. Since the tow yard is located near Murray Middle School, the sheriff’s office said it immediately activated an active-shooter response and placed the school on lockout as deputies responded to the scene. Road patrol deputies, aviation, detectives and other available units quickly began searching for the woman’s car, deputies said, and located the car traveling on Cove Road near U.S. 1 Deputies said they attempted a traffic stop but the driver fled, forcing deputies to perform a PIT maneuver, bringing the car to a stop. The individuals who were shot at left the area before deputies arrived, the sheriff’s office said. It is unclear whether any of them were struck by gunfire. The woman was taken into custody and transported to the sheriff’s office, where detectives are currently questioning her. Deputies said additional information will be provided as it becomes available.

Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms is on trial over allegations that he improperly influenced a city bidding process involving two vacant lots in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park area. Mimms faces charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors allege he steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included Mimms' niece and another city employee. On Thursday, much of the testimony focused on who controlled the RFP process and how closely Mimms remained involved after it was turned over to the city's purchasing department. FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails and other records collected during the investigation. One focus was the nearby Lincoln Theater and its need for parking. Brisky testified Mimms had told the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency that the RFP would include language addressing the theater's parking needs. But that language was not included in the request Mimms sent to the purchasing department. Brisky also testified investigators found no evidence Mimms filed a 2019 memorandum concerning the parking plans in the relevant city records. The defense questioned the significance of that omission and emphasized that the purchasing department was responsible for putting together and publishing the RFP after receiving the project's specifications. See also: NTSB report clarifies Amazon plane crash timeline that killed 5 on Sept. 6 Defense attorneys also challenged the state's characterization of the process as a sole-source arrangement. Brisky acknowledged the RFP was not technically a sole-source contract. The state, meanwhile, pointed to emails showing Mimms continued to communicate with city employees about the RFP, including its evaluation criteria and the evaluation committee. Other emails showed city employees knew there had been one submission after the RFP was posted. An LPYP email address was copied on one of those communications. The defense also questioned the investigation's treatment of other city employees involved in the process, including a purchasing official who was not charged. Later, former Fort Pierce employee Kalita Scott testified about LPYP and its efforts to develop the Lincoln Park properties. She described the organization as a group of young professionals focused on community development and said the need for parking near the Lincoln Theater was known in the community. Prosecutors allege Mimms manipulated the city's process to ensure LPYP received the lease. The defense has argued Mimms did not improperly favor the organization and that the evidence does not establish a criminal conspiracy. The trial is continuing in St.

Two women are in custody in Martin County after a shooting at a tow yard in Stuart led to a police chase and a violent crash. “I have more questions than I have answers,” said Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. Budensiek said the incident began around 1 p.m. when two women arrived at the tow yard to retrieve a car that had been towed earlier that morning. While they were there, two other individuals showed up to claim the same vehicle. “They got into some type of argument about the belongings in the car, which, by the way, the only thing in the car really was a couple of guns,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said one of the original women then grabbed a gun and began shooting. No one was injured, but bullets struck trailers in the yard. “It’s just crazy how it went down,” said Gary Reed, the owner of Gary’s Towing and Recovery. Reed, who was not present during the shooting, said his employee called him, screaming for help. And I’m running as fast as I can,” Reed said. https://www.facebook.com/MartinCountySheriffsOffice/posts/pfbid0enPBfuxCWxva9Ce6vmU7hGP3nKdhfidsLzp1e7zxkZ58uSYxB3KhHPTdVi9kagZnl By the time deputies and Reed arrived at the scene, all four individuals involved had fled. The sheriff said the accused shooter had taken the car they were disputing over, but deputies located her shortly after. She attempted to flee but was quickly arrested. Investigators identified her as Jade Rondon from Miami. The other woman she was with has been identified as Valerie Valdes, also from Miami. Budensiek said she was taken into custody after causing a violent collision on U.S. “Why she was driving at a high rate of speed, why she was weaving out of traffic, we’re not sure. We didn’t even know for sure that that car was involved at that time,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators are working to answer these questions and plan to obtain search warrants for the suspects’ cars and phones. He hopes to have more answers by next week. Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to repair a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and recent rain continue to affect parts of South Florida. Skid loaders were working along the narrow roadway beside the Indian River Lagoon, adding dirt and sand to reinforce an area where erosion has left the road’s edge vulnerable. Crews brought 32 loads of dirt to the site Sept. But only days later, the embankment again needed repairs. Resident Gene Barnes said the recurring work is not a long-term solution. We’re losing ground year by year, Barnes said. Until the Corps of Engineers or something like that comes and puts a headwall in to stabilize it, it’s not going to be an easy fix. The road has faced erosion problems before. Heavy rain damaged sections in 2014, and Hurricane Nicole caused additional washouts in 2022. Barnes said continued rain and tidal action could undermine the roadway itself. See also: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge If we keep getting rains like this, it’s going to undermine the road, and then the road is going to collapse and the school bus is going to fall in the hole, he said. The latest repairs follow an emergency sand operation at nearby Jetty Park that cost taxpayers nearly $500,000. While repairs on South Indian River Drive may be less costly, residents said the erosion is likely to remain a concern as more rain and tidal action are forecast.

Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

Lucie County mosquito control are working to stop mosquitoes from breeding after recent rain created standing water. In a residential neighborhood near U.S. 1 and Fort Pierce, mosquito control teams treated swales and used a backpack blower to distribute larvicide. Officials said the rain has increased standing water, which allows mosquito eggs to hatch. "So relative to last year, mosquito calls have been pretty reduced, but at any moment’s notice following a lot of rain, we can have a huge strike in population, so it's important to be on top of our game," said Daniel Tuzzolino, senior entomologist at St. Lucie County Mosquito Control. DENGUE FEVER: Dengue fever case in Palm Beach County prompts mosquito control action Kenneth Fusco, a nearby resident, shared his experience with the mosquito problem. "If I go out in my front yard and start to do anything, you get bit. I have an island behind me with some cats. If I go over there, I have to wear long pants because I get chewed to death," Fusco said. He added, "Park the truck and leave it for 20 minutes and leave it in front of my house, please!" Crews are also monitoring reports of dengue fever and West Nile virus in surrounding counties. They are asking residents to empty or remove containers holding water to prevent mosquito breeding. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "We are really doubling down and making sure that the people of St. Lucie County know the importance of tipping and tossing because anything that you do to remove potential environment for those dangerous mosquitoes really helps reduce the likelihood that we have transmission in this county," Tuzzolino said. Thursday's heavy rain also caused erosion and a washout along Indian River Drive, where crews were completing a shoulder repair project designed to protect the roadway during heavy rain events. More rain is expected, which could lead to additional standing water and, Tuzzolino said, "A lot more mosquitoes! A lot more mosquitoes!" If you are dealing with a mosquito problem near your home, contact St. Lucie County mosquito control at 772-462-1962 or email mosquito@stlucieco.org. A criminal case involving 36 rescued border collies in Martin County is moving forward. Paige O’Donnell faces 72 criminal charges — two for each dog rescued from her home. She was not present at her docket sounding Thursday afternoon in the Martin County courthouse, but I spoke with her attorney, Russell Ferraro. “At this point I can’t really say anything on her behalf for or against her,” Ferraro said. “We just got the discovery in the case yesterday. We’re organizing it, going through it, and we’ll take it from there.” It has been just under two months since Martin County deputies took 36 dogs out of O’Donnell’s feces-filled home on Aug. The county condemned it days after the Border Collies were rescued. Ferraro said O’Donnell is staying elsewhere while the house is under repair. O’Donnell faces an animal cruelty and improper confinement charge for each dog and has pleaded not guilty. “Everybody’s got a right to a fair trial and to due process,” Ferraro said. The next hearing in O’Donnell’s case is scheduled for Dec. While the outcome of the case remains uncertain, most of O’Donnell’s former dogs have found loving homes. According to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, 30 of the dogs have been adopted, five have gone or are about to go to animal rescues, and one remains up for adoption. Lucie and Colleen Tilley near Deltona each adopted one of the rescued border collies. Both say their new family members — now named Nadia and Leila — have had little trouble adjusting to their new lives. “She’s just has an endless amount of energy and just wants to expend it at all times,” Cale said. Cale said Nadia, named after a character from the show “New Girl,” goes to work with him every day and usually warms up to new people after they offer her a treat. “She’s just has an endless amount of energy and just wants to expend it at all times,” Cale said. “When I saw where they came from, I expected a lot more of a challenge,” he added. She wants to be out there and interacting with the world.” “There’s no off switch; it’s all go, go, go,” Tilley said, as Leila raced back and forth behind her in her backyard during a Zoom interview. “It’s really satisfying to see, actually. Just that she’s— she’s happy.” Tilley recalled how nervous Leila was when she first came home on Sept. “At first — like the first three days — it took her to be able to go out the doors— like when I opened the front door, she would run and hide under the bed,” Tilley said. “Now she just runs straight through the sliding glass door, or into it.” Cale and Tilley both said their new border collies have taken well to training as they work to shed old habits, like jumping onto countertops. “I think that’s how they got their food,” Tilley speculated. When Tilley thinks about the criminal case against Leila’s former owner, she wonders what went wrong. Tilley, who showed dogs with her family during her childhood, said she remembers O’Donnell and her outstanding reputation. Like she had very well-bred dogs, very well-trained dogs, beautiful dogs,” Tilley said. “And so all of us were just like, what happened?” Cale revealed that he’d been grieving the loss of his beloved Border Collie, Jessie, who’d died from cancer a year before he heard about what had happened in Palm City. “You just never know when the right dog is gonna come along, and this was the right dog,” Cale said. “(Jessie) was the ride-or-die that would have gone anywhere with me — roaming the woods and getting into mischief ... And that’s gonna be Nadia now.” “You just never know when the right dog is gonna come along, and this was the right dog,” Cale said. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says one Border Collie is still up for adoption. The Miami Dolphins confirmed earlier this week that running back De'Von Achane tore his ACL on Sunday and will miss the rest of the season.Achane was injured just five plays into Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs, leaving the game after an uncomfortable tackle.Head coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday that Achane has maintained a positive attitude but acknowledged the road ahead will not be easy."As far as how he's doing, he's had a great attitude. I'm sure he's going to have some tough moments," Hafley said. "There's going to be some really hard days and then there'll be some days where he's this positive, energetic self," Hafley said.Hafley said the recovery goes beyond the physical."Whenever you go through a serious injury, it's not just a physical recovery; it's mental. We got to make sure that he's doing OK, and that's very important to me," Hafley said.Without their star running back, the Dolphins are preparing for Week 4 against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings. So far this season, Miami has faced opponents that are all 3-0. Hafley said the team is focused on taking things one week at a time."Each week we just try to go 1-0 and not look ahead or behind. But we know we've played really good teams. And I think individually we went up against a lot of really good players. And I think we're gaining experience and we're getting better because of that," Hafley said.This week is no different, as the Dolphins hit the road again to face the undefeated Vikings."To get a chance to go there, and I think one of the better atmospheres in the NFL with a really good team and a really good staff, I think it's a huge challenge. But I think they've embraced it. I think we've all embraced it," Hafley said.The Dolphins will look to secure their first win of the season Sunday.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the incident unfolded shortly after 1 p.m. Friday at Gary's Towing and Recovery on Southeast Cove Road. Investigators said 23-year-old Jade Ely Rondon, of Miami, arrived at the tow yard to retrieve a BMW that had been towed earlier in the day. Deputies said another group arrived shortly afterward, leading to an altercation. According to the sheriff's office, Rondon retrieved a firearm and fired multiple shots at the other individuals before fleeing the scene in a vehicle. Because the business is located about a half-mile from Murray Middle School, deputies activated an active-shooter response and placed the school on lockout while officers searched for the suspect. Deputies later located Rondon's vehicle near U.S. 1 and attempted a traffic stop. Investigators said she refused to stop, prompting deputies to perform a PIT maneuver and take her into custody. Rondon was arrested and charged with two counts of aggravated assault with firearm, discharging a firearm in public, aggravated fleeing and eluding, driving while license suspended, and felony criminal mischief. See also: Woman arrested at Mar-a-Lago after claiming Sen. Tom Cotton invited her According to the sheriff's office, Valerie Valdes, 24, had accompanied Rondon to the tow yard to retrieve the BMW. After the shooting, deputies said Valdes fled in the vehicle they originally arrived in and drove recklessly while attempting to leave the area. Investigators said Valdes ultimately crashed at the intersection of Constitutional Boulevard and U.S. She was taken to Cleveland Clinic Martin South Hospital for treatment of her injuries before being arrested. Valdes is charged with operating an unregistered motor vehicle, and four counts of reckless driving with injuries. The people who were allegedly targeted by the gunfire left the towing facility before deputies arrived. CBS12 News spoke with Gary Reed, owner of Gary's Towing and Recovery, who said he's grateful no one was hurt during the incident. Murray Middle School sent out the following message to families: "Good afternoon, Lions! Please note that we have heavy police presence in the area for an incident unrelated to Murray. We are following Martin County Sheriff's Office guidance and are on a lock out. We will remain in close contact with them and provide additional information as it becomes available. Thank you, Principal Roth" The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active and additional charges are possible.

Two men are out of jail on bond after being arrested in two separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week, according to the Port St. According to an arrest affidavit, 23-year-old Giovanny Barthelemy was driving a silver Toyota Highlander around 8:40 p.m. Tuesday when it collided with a 16-year-old riding an electric motorcycle on Southwest Roma Way near Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at the community clubhouse recorded the crash. The officer wrote that the video shows the SUV turning into the community entrance as the teen crossed in front of it. The teen was thrown from the motorcycle. The affidavit says the SUV then backed up and drove away while the injured teen lay on the ground waving his arms. The teen was taken to Tradition Medical Center and then flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Police said he broke his left femur and hurt his left ankle, and he was listed in serious but stable condition. See also: Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Florida on domestic violence charges, enters not guilty plea One witness told police the electric motorcycle had no headlights. Two witnesses said both vehicles were going fast. The SUV's owner, the father of Barthelemy's girlfriend, called 911. He told police Barthelemy said he had hit someone on a bike and then driven home. Officers found Barthelemy at his home on Southwest Ridgecrest Drive. According to the affidavit, after being read his rights, Barthelemy told police he felt and heard the crash and knew right away he had hit a person. He told police he should have stopped but didn't, and said his phone was dead, according to the affidavit. Barthelemy is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries, which is a felony. He was also given a traffic citation. He was released on a $7,500 bond. The second case happened earlier that afternoon. Lucie officer clocked a silver Toyota going 85 mph in a 40-mph zone, according to an arrest affidavit. The officer turned around and tried to stop the car. The affidavit says the driver went over a concrete median into the opposite lanes, ran a red light, and hit a traffic sign at Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street before getting on northbound Interstate 95. The officer turned off his lights and siren but kept the car in sight. Police said the car later broke down on the side of I-95. Officers said the driver, 19-year-old Christian Johnson, got out and ran toward the back of the car. Lucie detective, a Florida Highway Patrol trooper, and the officer surrounded the car, and Johnson was taken into custody. According to the affidavit, Johnson's license had been suspended three times in St. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving and driving with a suspended or revoked license. All three charges are misdemeanors. He was released on a $12,500 bond. In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

Flooding continues to be a problem across Indiantown, leaving some residents questioning why the issue persists despite years of efforts to improve drainage. Large areas of the village saw flooding this week including Booker Park despite spending more than $2 million on drainage improvements in the area in recent years. Residents have seen some improvements over the years but believe more need to be done. I’ve been here almost 60 years and it hasn’t gotten right, Brown said. It is better than it was at some point, but in 60 years you would think it would be far greater than what it is now. The latest round of flooding has affected other parts of Indiantown as well. Oak River saw significant flooding this week, while floodwater also surrounded Indian River Middle School. For residents whose homes take on water, the problem can quickly become a financial burden. Flood insurance can help cover some flood-related damage, but it can also come with a significant cost. For homeowners without a flood policy, recovery can become more difficult. Brian Christensen, president of Coast to Coast Adjuster, said homeowners facing a flood claim without coverage may have to look for other ways to pay for repairs. See also: GALLERY: Ag Reserve meeting draws overflow crowd, tense atmosphere in Delray Beach If you don’t have a flood policy and it is a flood claim and your homeowners policy won’t cut it, I start looking for a loan, Christensen said. Start looking for something a second mortgage, friends, family, churches anything that can assist you. Indiantown Councilman Anthony Dowling said the village is working with Martin County on the flooding problem. The village is also considering a municipal bond that could help address broken pipes and other infrastructure issues. Dowling said the village is repairing pipes that are already damaged and clearing debris from drainage systems. He acknowledged that addressing the flooding problem will not happen overnight and urged residents to take precautions when floodwater is present. I would encourage no kids to play in the water, Dowling said. Village officials say they are continuing to look for ways to address flooding throughout Indiantown. But after years of flooding and millions of dollars spent on drainage improvements residents say they want to know when they will finally see a significant difference.

hero.headline: New I-95 Interchange at Oslo Road Opens a Year Early in Indian River County
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis opened a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, marking the completion of a roughly $100 million project finished a full year ahead of schedule. DeSantis called it a critical new connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region's growing population, and said it is the first new interchange built in this part of the state in almost 50 years.

DeSantis said the new exit is expected to ease congestion at the nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he said. With daily traffic on the corridor projected to keep growing through 2045, DeSantis said the project shows how the state can improve quality of life now while building capacity for the future.

The governor said the direct interstate connection will also speed up emergency response in southern Indian River County. "We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%," DeSantis said. "That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations." Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, a process that lets contractors propose ways to speed up construction in exchange for sharing in the savings. "This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially," Perdue said. "We're really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits." Perdue also said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region.

DeSantis said FDOT acquired nearby land for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat, which he said will be the only relocation site of its kind in Southeast Florida. "Florida [is] showing that it's possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship," DeSantis said. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recalled his surprise at how quickly the project came together. "When I got the phone call, I said, 'We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at,'" Flescher said. "This team worked an incredible operation." Flescher said the interchange addresses needs tied to the county's current growth, not just its future. "This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county," he said. "And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development."

cards.headline: Sheriff: Video Shows Teen Punching Into Truck Before Fatal Shooting at Garcia's Boat Ramp
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers says investigators are examining whether the shooting death of a 17-year-old at Garcia's Boat Ramp was self-defense, citing video of the teen punching into a truck before a shot was fired.
cards.body:
A 17-year-old was shot and killed Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense, according to Sheriff Eric Flowers. The shooting happened during a confrontation at the waterfront site, which authorities say has become a frequent gathering spot for teenagers.

Flowers said investigators reviewed video showing the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired. "The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck," Flowers said during a news conference. "That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case." The Indian River County Sheriff's Office released video of the confrontation that occurred moments before the shooting.

Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that firearms are raising the risks tied to those gatherings. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. "Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these."

Both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident, authorities said. As of Monday, no arrests had been made. "It's gonna be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed, but I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The investigation remains active, and the sheriff's office is asking anyone with video footage or information about the shooting, or about future teen meetup events, to contact investigators. Flowers also urged parents to know where their children are and suggested location-tracking tools as one way to help keep them safe.

hero.headline: State Says No Elevated Brain Cancer Rates in St. Lucie County; Mast Presses CDC
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health's St. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber says an updated review of cancer registry data through 2023 shows no sign of elevated brain cancer rates in the county, even as families continue to track new diagnoses, including three confirmed in August alone. The finding comes as Rep. Brian Mast renews his call for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the underlying data behind state conclusions.

"Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about," Sperber wrote, adding that the county's rates are in line with nearby counties and the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded, and he said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as one type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. A 2019 state review had examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983, finding no statistically significant increase and no designated cancer cluster, but that review did not include later diagnoses or the broader range of brain tumors families are now tracking.

Stephanie Ankiel, who helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast, has spent years mapping where patients lived in search of possible connections. Driving through Fort Pierce, she pointed to her late husband's childhood home and, a few houses away, a home where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor her husband, Mark Cunningham, first had: oligodendroglioma, which later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified a home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma 20 years apart, and elsewhere along the route she pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. Ankiel wants officials to examine the full range of brain cancers on her map, not just glioblastoma. The diagnoses and proximity of patients' homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause, and no environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause.

Mast said he has again asked the CDC to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. "You need to give us the receipts," Mast said. "Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place." The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns and confirmed it assisted Florida's investigation in 2018, but it did not address whether it had received Mast's latest request or would open a new review. A CDC spokesperson said the agency "is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health's request."

Matt Elliott, diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, said he initially believed his case was isolated until he met other local patients. "I thought I was the only one," he said. He has decided not to continue treatment and is instead spending his time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. "It might take them years to even figure out what the hell's going on around here," Elliott said. "I can't expect myself to be around at the end of it." He said he wants investigators to find answers but is focused on the life he has left. "I'm not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old," Elliott said. "But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun."
