cards.headline: Martin County border collie hoarding case moves forward, most dogs adopted
cards.teaser: Paige O'Donnell faces 72 criminal charges after 36 border collies were rescued from her Palm City home, with a December hearing ahead. Most of the dogs have already found new homes.
cards.body:
A criminal case against a Martin County woman accused of hoarding 36 border collies in a feces-filled home is moving forward, with a hearing scheduled for Dec. 1. Paige O'Donnell faces 72 criminal charges, two for each dog rescued from her home, including an animal cruelty charge and an improper confinement charge for each animal. She has pleaded not guilty.

O'Donnell was not present at her docket sounding Thursday afternoon at the Martin County courthouse. Her attorney, Russell Ferraro, said the defense received discovery materials in the case the day before. "At this point I can't really say anything on her behalf for or against her," Ferraro said. "We just got the discovery in the case yesterday. We're organizing it, going through it, and we'll take it from there." He added, "Everybody's got a right to a fair trial and to due process."

Martin County deputies removed the 36 border collies from O'Donnell's home in August. The county condemned the house days after the dogs were rescued, and Ferraro said O'Donnell is staying elsewhere while repairs are made. According to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, 30 of the dogs have been adopted, five have gone or are about to go to animal rescues, and one remains up for adoption.

Among the adopters are Cale and Colleen Tilley, who live near Deltona and each took in one of the rescued border collies, now named Nadia and Leila. Tilley said Leila was nervous when she first came home on Sept. 21, hiding under the bed when the front door opened, but has since become comfortable running through the house. "There's no off switch; it's all go, go, go," Tilley said. "It's really satisfying to see, actually. Just that she's happy." Tilley, who showed dogs with her family as a child, said she remembered O'Donnell's reputation in the dog show world. "(Paige) won everything. Like she had very well-bred dogs, very well-trained dogs, beautiful dogs," Tilley said. "And so all of us were just like, what happened?"

Cale said he adopted Nadia about a year after losing his previous border collie, Jessie, to cancer. He said Nadia goes to work with him daily and warms up to new people after receiving a treat. "You just never know when the right dog is gonna come along, and this was the right dog," Cale said. Both Cale and Tilley said their dogs are working through old habits, including jumping onto countertops, which Tilley speculated may stem from how the dogs previously got food.

cards.headline: Returning Stuart City Manager Michael Mortell Vows More Structure, Restored Trust
cards.teaser: Michael Mortell is back as Stuart city manager and says he plans to bring more administrative structure to City Hall after a year of commission division. In his first interview since officially returning Friday, he said he has unfinished business to address.
cards.body:
Michael Mortell is back in his role as Stuart city manager after officially returning to the position Friday. In his first interview since his return, Mortell said he still has more to give the city after being dismissed from the job last October.

"There's something drawing me. I feel the need to go back and finish the unwritten book or the unwritten chapter," Mortell said. "I felt like there was things that were left that needed to be corrected and needed to be finished."

After his dismissal, Mortell worked for the 19th Judicial Circuit, where he said he learned practices that could help the city run more efficiently. He said his focus now is on defining administrative roles and lines of authority at City Hall. "We need to really focus on defining administration defining what—who are the policymakers, who the administrators, who is the chain of command, and how we need to disseminate information," Mortell said. "Implementing more structure and defining it will help all of us make the city a better place and I think residents will know exactly what to expect."

Over the past year, a divided Stuart Commission and leadership turnover have left some residents questioning their confidence in city government. Resident David Kelman raised those concerns at a previous city commission meeting, telling commissioners, "You all represent this city. You need to step back and unite because what you're doing ain't going to work. It's three versus two here." Asked how he plans to restore the community's faith in city government, Mortell said it starts with teamwork. "We really identify everybody's strengths ... and find ways to work more as a team so that everybody feels like they're contributing to the outcome and that everybody has the common goal of what's best for Stuart in mind and rather than being divisive at all to try to find ways to work together," Mortell said. Mortell has a long history working for the city and is returning to the job with what he describes as a fresh approach.

hero.headline: Martin County hoarding case against Paige O'Donnell heads to Dec. 1 hearing
hero.body:
A criminal case against Paige O'Donnell, the Palm City woman accused in the hoarding of 36 border collies rescued from her Martin County home in August, is moving toward its next hearing on Dec. 1. O'Donnell faces 72 criminal charges, including an animal cruelty charge and an improper confinement charge for each of the 36 dogs. She has pleaded not guilty.

O'Donnell was not present at her docket sounding Thursday afternoon at the Martin County courthouse. Her attorney, Russell Ferraro, said the defense received discovery in the case the day before. "At this point I can't really say anything on her behalf for or against her," Ferraro said. "We just got the discovery in the case yesterday. We're organizing it, going through it, and we'll take it from there." Ferraro added, "Everybody's got a right to a fair trial and to due process."

Martin County deputies removed the 36 border collies from O'Donnell's feces-filled home in August. The county condemned the house days after the dogs were rescued, and Ferraro said O'Donnell is staying elsewhere while repairs continue. According to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, 30 of the rescued dogs have been adopted, five have gone or are about to go to animal rescues, and one remains up for adoption.

Among the adopters are Cale and Colleen Tilley, who each took in one of the rescued border collies, now named Nadia and Leila. Tilley said Leila was nervous when she first came home on Sept. 21 and hid under the bed when the front door opened, but now runs straight through the sliding glass door. "There's no off switch; it's all go, go, go," Tilley said. "It's really satisfying to see, actually. Just that she's— she's happy." Cale said Nadia has an "endless amount of energy" and goes to work with him every day, usually warming up to new people after they offer her a treat. He had been grieving the loss of his previous border collie, Jessie, who died of cancer a year before he learned about the dogs rescued in Palm City. "You just never know when the right dog is gonna come along, and this was the right dog," Cale said. Tilley, who showed dogs with her family as a child and knew O'Donnell's reputation for well-bred, well-trained show dogs, said she still wonders what led to the case. "(Paige) won everything. Like she had very well-bred dogs, very well-trained dogs, beautiful dogs," Tilley said. "And so all of us were just like, what happened?"

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Man Sentenced to Probation for Hiding Gun in June Shooting
cards.teaser: Christopher Williams Jr. has pleaded no contest to hiding the firearm used in a June shooting on North 19th Street, while the man accused of pulling the trigger still faces no charges.
cards.body:
Christopher Williams Jr., 19, of Fort Pierce, pleaded no contest on Sept. 3 to charges of false statement to law enforcement and tampering with evidence, according to court documents in St. Lucie County. The charges stemmed from a shooting on the 500 block of North 19th Street on June 2. As part of a plea agreement with the State Attorney's Office, Williams Jr. was sentenced to six months of probation and ordered to pay court costs. He had faced a maximum penalty of six years in state prison and a $6,000 fine.

Investigators said that after the June 2 shooting, Williams Jr. told Fort Pierce Police Department officers that he was inside his home at the time and was not aware a shooting had taken place. Officers were told by a witness that Williams Jr. had been given the gun after 18-year-old Ja'Shawn Crosby shot his 17-year-old girlfriend following an altercation. In a second interview with police, Williams Jr. admitted he hid the firearm on the property before Crosby left the scene.

On July 8, the State Attorney's Office declined to pursue an attempted second-degree murder charge against Crosby, saying there was not sufficient evidence to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. Crosby has not been charged in connection with the shooting.

Williams Jr.'s plea closes out the case against him over his role in concealing the weapon, while the underlying shooting that injured the 17-year-old girl remains without any criminal charges filed against the man accused of firing the gun.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County finds 13 unpermitted license plate readers, gives owners 30 days
hero.body:
St. Lucie County staff discovered 13 license plate reader cameras installed in public rights-of-way without permits, according to County Communications Director Erick Gill. The discovery came after a Wednesday, Sept. 30 deadline set by the Florida Department of Transportation for municipalities to remove license plate readers from state-controlled roads.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has claimed three of the 13 cameras and is working to find out why they were not permitted. The county says it has 53 permitted license plate readers on its rights-of-way, a number separate from the 13 unpermitted units staff found.

"We don't know who they belong to," Gill said. "They were just put in our right-of-way."

"We were surprised, you know, that were that many out there," Gill said.

One of the unpermitted cameras was found near a gas station off Orange Avenue and 25th Street in Fort Pierce. Ricky Mathura, who works at the gas station, said he did not know why the camera was there.

County staff is actively working to identify the owners of the remaining unclaimed readers and has taped notices on the cameras directing owners to remove them within 30 days. Once that 30-day window closes, Gill said staff will move to take the cameras down.

"We'll begin the process of either removing them if we feel like we can safely remove them without damaging the equipment and endangering our staff, or at least covering up so the cameras can't capture any surveillance," Gill said.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Clerk: Board Relied on Mimms for Accurate Information
cards.teaser: City Clerk Linda Cox testified on day three of former city manager Nick Mimms' corruption trial that the city board relied on him to provide correct information regarding a land deal involving his niece.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox testified Wednesday as the corruption trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. Cox told the jury that city board members relied on Mimms to give them accurate information, confirming to Assistant State Attorney Brandon White that the board expected correct information from him and depended on him to provide it.

The jury viewed video evidence of a series of city meetings, including one from October 2019 in which a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presented a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, was among the organization's board members, along with a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared surplus even though it had been designated for parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater. Footage from later meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency showed the board voting to declare the lots surplus before the Lincoln Park Young Professionals were announced as the winning bidder.

Under cross-examination by defense attorney Donald Murrell, Cox acknowledged it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking the property. Murrell asked Cox whether she knew the individuals involved were city employees.

Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee.According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater.Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information."Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?" Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said."Yes," Cox said."Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?" Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said."Yes," Cox said.Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid.WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city managerUnder cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time."You knew they were city employees," Murrell said."I did," Cox said."And it bothered you that they were doing this?" Murrell said."I thought it was a little odd," Cox said."You didn't raise any objections," Murrell said."I did not," Cox said.Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney's presence at the meetings."He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?" Murrell said."Yes," Cox said."He didn't raise any objections or concerns, did he?" Murrell said."Not at the meeting," Cox said."Ever?" Murrell said."I wouldn't know. Not that I know of," Cox said.The trial is expected to last at least a week.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Crews Repair South Indian River Drive Erosion Again
cards.teaser: Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to fix a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and rain keep battering the road along the Indian River Lagoon.
cards.body:
Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to repair a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and recent rain continue to affect parts of South Florida. Skid loaders worked along the narrow roadway beside the Indian River Lagoon, adding dirt and sand to reinforce an area where erosion has left the road's edge vulnerable.

Crews had already brought 32 loads of dirt to the site in September. Only days later, the embankment again needed repairs, forcing the same stretch of road to be shored up for a second time within a week.

Resident Gene Barnes said the recurring work is not a long-term solution. "We're losing ground year by year," Barnes said. "Until the Corps of Engineers or something like that comes and puts a headwall in to stabilize it, it's not going to be an easy fix."

The road has faced erosion problems before. Heavy rain damaged sections in 2014, and Hurricane Nicole caused additional washouts in 2022. Barnes warned that continued rain and tidal action could undermine the roadway itself. "If we keep getting rains like this, it's going to undermine the road, and then the road is going to collapse and the school bus is going to fall in the hole," he said. The latest repairs follow an emergency sand operation at nearby Jetty Park that cost taxpayers nearly $500,000. While repairs on South Indian River Drive may be less costly, residents said the erosion is likely to remain a concern as more rain and tidal action are forecast.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie TikTok Creator Jailed as Computer-Access Case Reopens
cards.teaser: Mark Stephen Asea, a Port St. Lucie man who describes himself as a cybersecurity engineer on TikTok, was jailed after police reopened an investigation into claims he accessed women's devices and shared private information in his videos.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man whose TikTok and Twitch bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation into him that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records, with bond set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped.

The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women's electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile's bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman's password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking.

The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts.

The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea's booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

hero.headline: Martin County Issues Advisory After Sentinel Chickens Test Positive for West Nile Virus
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County has issued an advisory to residents after several sentinel chickens tested positive for West Nile virus. The department is coordinating with Martin County Mosquito Control on enhanced surveillance of mosquitoes and diseases, along with targeted mosquito treatment to reduce the risk of transmission.

The health department said anyone experiencing fever, chills, sweats, nausea or vomiting, and headache should seek immediate medical attention.

Residents are urged to take basic precautions including spraying on mosquito repellent, covering arms and legs with clothing, and draining standing water. The department noted mosquitoes breed in standing water, and as little as one bottle cap of water sitting for more than a week is enough for them to multiply.

cards.headline: Both Port St. Lucie Hit-and-Run Suspects Now Free on Bond
cards.teaser: A 23-year-old driver accused of fleeing after a teen on an e-motorcycle broke his femur and a 19-year-old accused of leading police on an 85 mph chase have both posted bond in separate Port St. Lucie cases.
cards.body:
Two men arrested in separate Port St. Lucie hit-and-run cases this week are now out of jail after posting bond, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. One case involved a 16-year-old left with a broken femur after being struck while riding an electric motorcycle, and the other involved a driver who fled from police at 85 mph before crashing.

According to an arrest affidavit, 23-year-old Giovanny Barthelemy was driving a silver Toyota Highlander around 8:40 p.m. Tuesday when it collided with the teen on Southwest Roma Way near Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at a community clubhouse recorded the crash, showing the SUV turning into the community entrance as the teen crossed in front of it. The teen was thrown from the motorcycle, and the affidavit says the SUV backed up and drove away while he lay on the ground waving his arms. He was taken to Tradition Medical Center and then flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was listed in serious but stable condition with a broken left femur and an injured left ankle. One witness told police the electric motorcycle had no headlights, and two witnesses said both vehicles were traveling fast. The SUV's owner, the father of Barthelemy's girlfriend, called 911 after Barthelemy told him he had hit someone on a bike and driven home. Officers found Barthelemy at his home on Southwest Ridgecrest Drive, where he told them, after being read his rights, that he felt and heard the crash and knew immediately he had hit a person. He said he should have stopped but didn't, and that his phone was dead. Barthelemy was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries, a felony, along with a traffic citation. He was released on a $7,500 bond.

The second case happened earlier that same afternoon. A St. Lucie officer clocked a silver Toyota going 85 mph in a 40-mph zone and tried to stop the car, according to an arrest affidavit. The driver went over a concrete median into oncoming lanes, ran a red light, and hit a traffic sign at Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street before merging onto northbound Interstate 95. The officer turned off his lights and siren but kept the car in sight as it later broke down on the side of I-95. The driver, 19-year-old Christian Johnson, got out and ran toward the back of the car before a St. Lucie detective, a Florida Highway Patrol trooper, and the officer surrounded the vehicle and took him into custody. According to the affidavit, Johnson's license had been suspended three times. He was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving, and driving with a suspended or revoked license, all misdemeanors. He was released on a $12,500 bond.

In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Sabol Resigns Amid Union Fight Over Hazing Firings
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol has submitted a 90-day resignation notice as the district battles its firefighters' union over the firing of three employees in a hazing case involving a modified bug zapper.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol submitted a 90-day resignation notice Wednesday, stepping down as the district fights its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookie firefighters. Sabol confirmed she submitted the notice Wednesday and said her last work day will be December 31, 2026. She has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining.

"My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol said. St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement that Sabol is eligible for retirement and that the notice provides for her continued service during the 90-day period. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters," the statement said.

Sabol's departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters, demanding arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel. The union argues there was no just cause for the discipline. The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees.

Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Gives Notice Amid Hazing Arbitration Fight
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency fights its firefighters' union over the firing of three employees and suspension of two others in a hazing case. Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. "My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol said. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026."

St. Lucie County Fire Rescue confirmed the notice in a statement. "Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," the statement said. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters."

Sabol's departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp has said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. "There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp said.

The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

cards.teaser: Both men were released on bond after separate hit-and-run arrests this week, and Port St. Lucie police are reminding drivers they are legally required to stop for crashes and traffic stops.
cards.body:
Two men arrested in separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week have both been released on bond, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. The arrests come as the department issued a renewed warning that drivers are legally required to stop, whether for a traffic stop or after a crash.

In the first case, police said 23-year-old Giovanni Barthelemy hit a teenager riding an e-bike Wednesday near Southwest Roma Way and Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at a community entrance recorded the crash. Police said the video shows the driver trying to turn into the community, hitting the teen, then making a U-turn and driving away without calling 911 or stopping to help. The teen was badly hurt and taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Police said the car's owner later called 911 after the car came back home damaged, and that the owner was not driving at the time of the crash. Investigators then identified Barthelemy as the driver. He is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries and was released on a $7,500 bond.

The second case began Tuesday, when officers with the department's Traffic Unit tried to pull over a car near Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street. Police said the driver took off and hit a traffic sign while getting away. Officers later found the car on Interstate 95 and arrested 19-year-old Christian Johnson. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving, and driving with a suspended or revoked license. He was released on a $12,500 bond.

In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

hero.headline: 60-Day Rabies Alert Covers Part of Stuart After Raccoon Tests Positive
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a 60-day rabies alert Wednesday for part of Stuart after a raccoon captured off South Kanner Highway tested positive for rabies. The raccoon was captured Sunday, and health officials say the alert is now in effect for an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west.

Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in that area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. Officials noted an animal carrying rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively, making it hard to identify by sight alone.

People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030. Officials said treatment given after an exposure can prevent the disease from developing. Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and also notify Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211. Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods.

Health officials recommended several precautions for residents in and around the alert area. They advised keeping pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations, keeping pets leashed and under direct supervision, and avoiding handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Officials also urged residents not to leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors and to take steps to prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Anyone who encounters a wild animal that appears sick or injured was told to contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing the animal into a home. More information on rabies precautions is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies.

hero.headline: Stuart Rabies Alert Issued After Raccoon Tests Positive Near South Kanner Highway
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a 60-day rabies alert Wednesday for part of Stuart after a raccoon captured off South Kanner Highway tested positive for the disease. The raccoon was captured Sunday and later confirmed to have rabies, according to the department.

The alert zone covers an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies is present among wild animals in that area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife.

Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly spread through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. Officials said an animal with rabies may appear healthy and can act unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030. Treatment given after an exposure can prevent the disease from developing.

Health officials recommended that residents keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations, keep pets leashed and under direct supervision, and avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. They also advised against leaving pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors and urged residents to prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Anyone who encounters a wild animal in need of help was advised to contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing the animal into a home. Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211. Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Resigns Amid Hazing Arbitration Fight
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol has submitted her 90-day notice of resignation, stepping down as the agency faces a contested arbitration fight with its firefighters union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday, saying her employment agreement requires 90 days notice because it is a 3-year contract. Her last work day will be December 31, 2026. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute.

Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement that the District Attorney is eligible for retirement and that the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters," the statement said.

Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp has said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. "There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp said.

The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation.

Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

hero.headline: Medical Examiner Rules Port Salerno Toddler's Drowning an Accident
hero.body:
A medical examiner has ruled the death of 23-month-old Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo an accidental drowning, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Wednesday, a day after the boy was found in a pond on his family's property in Port Salerno. Deputies said Pablo was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing, began searching, and found him in the pond. Family members said the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office.

Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children at the time. He said a fence had once surrounded the pond but had broken down over time and was no longer functional. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two-year-old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital, where he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. Criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and reviewed the circumstances of the death before the medical examiner's ruling. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. He added that investigators found no signs the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," he said.

Budensiek is urging parents to enroll young children in swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision remains the most important way to prevent drownings. She recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents, along with swim instruction starting at a young age. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

Family members remember Pablo for his bright smile and joyful spirit. Relative Virginia Maldonado said she hopes people remember him by his smile and keep the family in their prayers. A GoFundMe has been established to help the family with expenses following his death.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Resigns as Firefighters Vote on Chief's Future
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District attorney Kim Sabol resigned Wednesday, minutes after a tense special fire board meeting exposed a gap in district policy over who investigates complaints against the district's own top leaders. Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to an alleged hazing investigation that has roiled the district for months. Firefighters are now casting ballots in a vote of no confidence against Fire Chief Jeff Lee as the fallout continues.

Nearly a dozen people spoke at Wednesday's special meeting, which board members called to address what they described as a major gap in district policy. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said the district has never had a policy spelling out how complaints against its own leaders, including the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney, should be handled. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said. "They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy.

The controversy stems from an alleged hazing incident reported earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, were fired as a result. Hutchinson said the incident was "just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun." Boudrias said "we're all still friends" and that there was "no ill intent" involving the victims. Months before the incident became public, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Chief Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the same district officials named in it, which Fowler said was "not a good process."

Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and said he welcomes any investigation from any agency. Of Sabol's resignation, Lee called it a "sad day" and said she "has been a tremendous attorney for the district." On the no-confidence vote, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over. "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said, adding "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Retired fire captain Mike Jenkins said people at the meeting "want action," and one attendee said "this system is so broken." As the firefighters union continues its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin, Fowler said the board may have authority to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work, saying she plans to raise the question with the board in a week. Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote against Lee.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man gets probation for hiding gun used in June shooting
cards.teaser: Christopher Williams Jr. pleaded no contest to hiding the firearm used in a June shooting on North 19th Street, while the man accused of pulling the trigger has not been charged.
cards.body:
Christopher Williams Jr., 19, of Fort Pierce, pleaded no contest on Sept. 3 to charges of false statement to law enforcement and tampering with evidence in connection with a shooting on the 500 block of North 19th Street on June 2. Under a plea agreement with the State Attorney's Office, Williams Jr. will serve six months of probation and was ordered to pay court costs. He had faced a maximum penalty of six years in a state prison and a $6,000 fine.

According to court documents in St. Lucie County, Williams Jr. initially told Fort Pierce Police Department officers that he was inside his home during the shooting and was not aware it had happened. Officers were told by a witness that Williams Jr. was given the gun after 18-year-old Ja'Shawn Crosby shot his 17-year-old girlfriend following an altercation. In a second interview with police, Williams Jr. admitted he hid the firearm on the property before Crosby left the scene.

Crosby has not been charged in the shooting. On July 8, the State Attorney's Office declined to pursue an attempted second-degree murder charge against him, saying there was not sufficient evidence to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

The plea deal closes out the case against Williams Jr. over his role in concealing the weapon, while the shooting itself remains without charges filed against the man accused of firing the gun.

hero.headline: Medical Examiner Rules Port Salerno Toddler's Drowning Accidental
hero.body:
The Martin County Medical Examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy in Port Salerno an accidental drowning. Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in a pond on his family's property near Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the child's parents called 911, calling it one of the most heart wrenching calls deputies can receive.

According to investigators, Pablo was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he slipped out of sight for a short time. When his mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and found him in the pond. Family members told investigators Pablo had been out of sight no more than 10 minutes. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, where he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts.

Budensiek said a fence had once stood around the pond but had been trampled down or broken over time, leaving it not functional. Martin County Sheriff's Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and found no indication anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said.

Charlene Lyons, President and CEO of YMCA Treasure Coast, said she was devastated when she heard the news. "I started at the Y as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me," Lyons said. She encouraged the public to contact the YMCA for information about swimming lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer, it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status, it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons said. Information about swimming lessons is available through the YMCA Treasure Coast website. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol Gives 90-Day Notice
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her 90-day notice Wednesday, announcing her exit as the agency fights its firefighters' union over the firing of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday, saying it was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026."

Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline.

The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp has said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing.

The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. The district has declined further comment while the contractual proceedings are ongoing. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Clerk Testifies Board Relied on Mimms in Avenue D Deal
cards.teaser: City Clerk Linda Cox testified on day three of former city manager Nick Mimms' corruption trial that the Fort Pierce board relied on Mimms for accurate information during the Avenue D land deal.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the corruption trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct tied to a land deal involving vacant lots on Avenue D.

The jury first heard from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. "Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?" White asked. "Yes," Cox said. "Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?" White asked. "Yes," Cox said. Attorneys also showed footage from later meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid.

Under cross-examination, defense attorney Donald Murrell argued it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking to obtain the property, and questioned Cox about whether she raised concerns at the time. "You knew they were city employees," Murrell said. "I did," Cox said. "And it bothered you that they were doing this?" Murrell said. "I thought it was a little odd," Cox said. "You didn't raise any objections," Murrell said. "I did not," Cox said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney's presence at the meetings. "He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?" Murrell said. "Yes," Cox said. "He didn't raise any objections or concerns, did he?" Murrell said. "Not at the meeting," Cox said. "Ever?" Murrell said. "I wouldn't know. Not that I know of," Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

hero.headline: Rabies Alert Issued in Stuart After Raccoon Tests Positive
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a 60-day rabies alert Wednesday after a raccoon captured in Stuart tested positive for the disease. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later confirmed positive for rabies, according to the department.

The alert covers an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies is present among wild animals in that area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly spread through the bite or scratch of an infected animal, and officials noted an infected animal may appear healthy while behaving unusually friendly or aggressively.

Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030. Treatment given after an exposure can prevent the disease from developing. Officials recommended that residents keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations, keep pets leashed and under direct supervision, avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals, and avoid leaving pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. They also advised preventing bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings, and contacting a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home.

Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211. Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies.

cards.headline: Medical Examiner Rules Port Salerno Toddler's Pond Drowning Accidental
cards.teaser: A medical examiner has ruled the death of 23-month-old Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, who drowned in a pond on his family's Port Salerno property Tuesday, an accidental drowning. Martin County's sheriff and a local swim school leader are renewing calls for supervision, pool fencing and swim lessons.
cards.body:
Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, a 23-month-old boy, drowned Tuesday evening in a pond on his family's property along Darling Street in Port Salerno, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The Martin County Medical Examiner has since ruled the death an accidental drowning following an autopsy, Sheriff John Budensiek said Wednesday.

According to the sheriff's office, the boy was outside with family members shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children nearby. The mother and aunt realized the boy was missing, began searching, and found him in the pond. Family members told investigators he had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. He was taken to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital, where he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts.

Budensiek said a fence had once surrounded the pond but had broken down over time and was no longer functional. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two year old did not know how to swim." MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene as part of the review. Budensiek said the investigation found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," he said. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning."

Budensiek encouraged parents to enroll young children in swim lessons, noting the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision remains the most important way to prevent drownings, along with door alarms, locked pool gates and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is equally critical. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to begin lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

hero.headline: Florida's Minimum Wage Hits Final Scheduled Increase to $15 an Hour
hero.body:
Florida's minimum wage rose to $15 an hour this week, marking the fourth and final increase under a schedule approved by voters through a 2020 referendum. The minimum wage for tipped workers also increased, rising to $11.98 an hour. Starting in 2027, the state minimum wage will no longer follow the fixed schedule and will instead be adjusted annually for inflation.

Workers say the new wage still falls short of covering the cost of living. A young man named Neff, speaking on Clematis Street on Wednesday, said the wage increase does not keep pace with rising expenses. "Minimum wage is going up but so is everything going up," he said. "You have to have another hustle, or another job so that way you can create more revenue and income for your family; $15 an hour is not enough." In South Florida, where housing and daily expenses run high, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology report found that a $25-an-hour wage is considered livable.

The wage hike is also putting pressure on small business owners who have to cover higher labor costs. John Ries, owner of Hot Pie Pizza in West Palm Beach, said he cannot fully absorb the increase without adjusting his prices. "I have to pass that cost on to the consumer; I cannot absorb a 7% increase in labor," Ries said. He said it is his policy to pay employees above the minimum wage, but rising costs across every part of his business make it difficult to keep prices low for customers.

With the scheduled increases now complete, future adjustments to Florida's minimum wage will depend on inflation rates starting in 2027. Workers like Neff say they will continue relying on multiple jobs or additional income sources to keep up with the cost of living, while business owners like Ries say they will keep watching labor costs as a factor in pricing decisions.

cards.headline: Florida Rolls Out Redesigned Driver's Licenses at Service Centers Statewide
cards.teaser: Florida began issuing new driver's license and identification card designs at service centers statewide on Wednesday, but current license holders do not need to replace their cards right away.
cards.body:
Florida began rolling out redesigned driver's licenses and identification cards at service centers statewide on Wednesday. The new cards feature Florida-themed imagery, including the historic Castillo de San Marcos fort in St. Augustine and the Discovery Space Shuttle.

The redesign also includes smaller details worked into the card's layout. An orange is integrated into the design as the "o" in Florida, and an alligator appears inside the REAL ID star printed in the top-right corner of the new licenses.

Current license holders do not need to replace their existing cards because of the redesign. The state will phase out the old card design over time, meaning both the old and new versions will be in circulation as Floridians renew or replace their licenses through the normal process.

The updated designs are now available at service centers across the state as part of the rollout that started Wednesday.
